After over four and a half years, Russia has been unable to convert its immense military sacrifices in Ukraine into meaningful military gains. But although Putin has no victories to present to the Russian people, he is not facing any real political precarity. One interpretation of CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s recent visit to Moscow was that he went, in part, to convince Putin that continuing the war is futile. If Ratcliffe thought he could get Putin to desist, he was indulging in wishful thinking. Rather than inching toward a conclusion, the war is escalating. It is not forcing Putin into a dead end either politically or militarily, and to expect Russian concessions or a negotiated settlement in the near to medium term would be folly.
The war, which Putin launched expecting a quick and complete victory, was not an accident. The decision to invade emanated from within the political order Putin has fashioned, a system that has been hardened by the war more than it has been transformed. The upcoming parliamentary elections that begin September 18 will certainly give the appearance of lockstep support for Putin. The reality is, of course, more complicated. But for outside observers, the key to understanding Putinism is its inner coherence, not the distance between stage-managed appearances and the actualities of public opinion. Day-to-day shifts on the frontlines in Ukraine and rhetorical expressions of domestic discontent are not among Putin’s major concerns. Despite its many costs, the war has bolstered Putinism and has been woven into the fabric of Russian statehood.
Analysts of Russia are understandably preoccupied by possible changes in the country’s internal trajectory—a burst of dissent, an election, a particularly destructive Ukrainian strike. Since the war began, the United States and Europe have expected its mounting costs to weigh down and even imperil Putin. Yet throughout the war, calm has reigned within Russia. A few weeks of panic directly followed the invasion of Ukraine, but after that, Russians withdrew into acceptance of the war. The 2023 mutiny by Yevgeny Prigozhin, the chief of the Wagner paramilitary company, led not to revolution but to his own untimely death. To the extent that polling can be trusted in Russia, Putin is vastly more popular than German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, French President Emmanuel Macron, or President Donald Trump are in their respective countries.
Ahead of the parliamentary elections, the Kremlin has barred the antiwar political party Yabloko from participating just as it was gaining support, and it has sentenced Lev Shlosberg, an antiwar political figure, to an 11-year prison term. Such repressive moves are routine in Putin’s Russia, the default operations of a governing system that long ago neutralized contests between political visions or clashes of rival parties. Not only have party politics vanished from Russia without much visible objection, there is no antiwar movement at all. Many Russians may not regard Putin’s regime as solicitous of the public good, which could explain the withdrawal of capital from the country, but the regime is also accepted as a given, a distant presence impervious to outside influence.
Before the war, Putin had spent decades disabling the channels of political opposition and of political action independent from the state. Two intersecting trends have marked his quarter century in power: the steady consolidation of his rule and the increasing militarization of Russia. The Putin who became Russia’s president in 2000 could seem to be many things at once: a modernizer, a reformer, and a strongman. But no matter how he framed his leadership, his instinct for power was acute—and power, for him, was always synonymous with control. From the start, he steadily expanded his control over the state, the media, and business. By 2012, when he was elected Russia’s president for the third time, he had the controlling stake in all three sectors.
Putin tied his ascent to the elimination of resistance. His progress toward dominance over Russia was gradual and linear: he took over the national television networks, disempowered regions that might have had friction with Moscow, forced oligarchs to give up their political ambitions, and turned all political parties into empty vessels. Deprived of their political clout, oligarchs were reduced to his monied vassals. A drawn-out struggle against the most prominent critic of his rule, the opposition figure Alexei Navalny, culminated in Navalny’s 2024 death in detention. After 2022, most of Russia’s remaining independent media outlets, along with hundreds of thousands of antiwar citizens, fled into exile; any critics who remained in Russia faced the threat of persecution. By now, the absence of meaningful dissent is simply the status quo.
Putin used his power to militarize the state and society, a trend that, in turn, augmented his hold on power. He invested heavily in defense. He made the commemoration of the World War II victory foundational to the country’s identity and encouraged the militarization of the Russian Orthodox Church. By the time he invaded Ukraine in 2022, the operation was vocally supported by Patriarch Kirill and most of the church’s clergy. Before then, Putin had launched many wars and military operations—in Chechnya, in Georgia, in Ukraine eight years earlier, and in Syria. He had avoided putting Russia on a wartime footing while making war itself a constant. And so, to Russians, war became familiar but not intrusive. From the beginning of his presidency, Putin had defined Russia in heroic terms, glorifying himself as the leader who restored it to its proper status as a respected great power. After 2022, this heroic depiction of Russia acquired a much more openly militaristic tenor.
The gradual accumulation of wars that could be depicted as at least partially successful—and which did not trouble Russians’ standard of living or sense of security—contributed to Russians’ toleration of a war in Ukraine that has lasted far longer than anyone initially expected. For the past four years, the Kremlin’s mission has been to convince Russians that the war is anything but an emergency. It is a necessary state of affairs, given Russia’s many enemies, and proper, given Russia’s mission and power.
Russian politics is not an edifice without cracks. Discontent with the war is gathering beneath the frozen surface. According to polls conducted on August 9 by the Levada Institute, many Russians would prefer peace talks to an ongoing war. Some business owners and workers, especially in small and medium-sized enterprises, are frustrated by sharp tax increases. Should the economy worsen and the war cast a darker shadow on daily life, this discontent could deepen. So far, the cracks remain small. Klepach’s criticism was a modest gesture of public dissent against an edifice of power that remains more than formidable. Putin has the institutional and practical means to do what he wishes. What he wishes, most of all, is to wage war.
At the center of Putin’s governing intent is subjugating Ukraine and forcing the West to accept that outcome. “Sooner or later, Ukraine will lose [its] western territories,” Putin predicted in his July speech to the navy. This was not a throwaway line. He meant that Russia is destined to control eastern Ukraine, while Poland, Hungary, and Romania will absorb the country’s west; in time, Ukraine will cease to exist. Ukraine’s nonexistence was the thesis of an essay he published seven months before the invasion. He has not moderated or mellowed over the past four years. If anything, Putinism has become more radical over time as it has become more secure; the war is a paradoxical source of the system’s self-confidence.
Unable to conceive of losing, Putin feels little pressure to make concessions. He has not run out of military options and may truly believe he can win. Russia’s sizable military has enough manpower to sustain a war of attrition and enough productive capacity to generate massive amounts of missiles and drones. The country has survived being severed, via sanctions and the difficulties of cross-border travel, from Europe and the United States. The Russian economy has suffered as a result of its warped relations with the outside world, particularly its broken relationship to Europe, its natural trading partner, but Russians have no political instruments with which to act on their grievances. They are observers to decision-making that cannot be publicly scrutinized. Inside the Kremlin, Russia’s considerable wealth is an unrestricted asset for Putin. It affords him the means to reward friends, indoctrinate Russian youth, and wage war in perpetuity.
Indeed, Putin might prefer an unending war, miserable as the prospect might sound, to the compromises entailed in a negotiated settlement that does not equal Ukraine’s surrender. In his July meeting with naval soldiers, he sounded as if he cannot see beyond the enormity of the war: “We should think together about how to preserve this [spirit of wartime struggle] for the future,” he observed. It would be madness for Russia to initiate a full-scale conventional war with European countries, but Moscow is intensifying its undeclared unconventional war through acts of sabotage in Europe. The war’s extension to Russian soil may even bolster support for Putin, stoking a defensive patriotism, especially among Russians who loathe “the West.” For years, Putin has inculcated the idea that “the collective West” is bent on harming Russia. Now he can claim to be vindicated.
The Kremlin can present demonstrations of military power, even without a victory, as proof of Russian independence in international affairs—sovereignty, in Putin’s parlance. Europe and the United States cannot tell Russia what to do. They cannot expel Russia’s armies from Ukraine or change the Kremlin’s calculus through economic pressure. Boris Yeltsin’s Russia had struggled to avoid NATO enlargement. Putin, who regards Yeltsin and Mikhail Gorbachev before him as weak leaders, has pushed for militarization as a means of ensuring Russia’s ability to say no to Europe and the United States. His emphasis on Russia’s autonomy is not a personal whim. It undergirds his domestic popularity.
Despite his place at the helm of a lavishly funded military-industrial complex, Putin is not especially skilled at strategy. There is a hollowness to his foreign policy: he has difficulty coordinating coercion with persuasion and great difficulty building relationships that have long-term legitimacy. The fall of Nicolás Maduro left Russia with little influence in Venezuela. The ouster of the Syrian dictator Bashar al-Assad led Damascus to curtail Russia’s military presence on the eastern Mediterranean. Russian power is ebbing in Central Asia, in Moldova, in Azerbaijan, and, lately, in Armenia (although not in Georgia), and Russia has won independence from Europe and the United States at the price of increased dependence on China—a risky bet.
Nowhere is the hollowness of Russian foreign policy more visible than in Ukraine. Russia is impossibly far from the victory Putin imagined in February 2022—controlling the country’s whole territory and populace. Putin can wreak havoc in Ukraine and may be able to establish a cease-fire he can accept, but he cannot conquer Ukraine. And an unconquered Ukraine will, by fighting or by remembering the horrors of Russia’s invasion, pose an enduring strategic challenge for Russia. Putin likely assumes that Europe will tire of supporting Ukraine. But for four and a half years, the trend has clearly gone the other way. The more suffering Russia inflicts on Ukrainian civilians, the more Europe invests in Ukraine’s defense and its own.
Yet all these challenges are not unmanageable for Putin. Whether Russia makes mistakes or serves Russians’ quotidian interests is secondary to his project of strengthening state power in and of itself. The conundrum of Putinism is that strategic mediocrity can enhance the regime’s durability—if not forever, then for quite a while. The more Russia is said to inhabit a hostile world, the more it finds itself wedded to an autocrat enamored of force.
Contemplating the solidity of Putin’s regime, analysts sometimes entertain fantasies of a more docile successor. The Kremlin, which surely has succession plans, cannot guarantee that they will be followed in the event of Putin’s death or departure from power. Yet Putinism is relatively well positioned to survive the career of its founder. Opposition movements and revolutions demand organization. (Organization was one of Vladimir Lenin’s greatest skills, which helped him lead the only successful revolution from below in Russian history.) Inchoate discontent must contend with the vast security services that Putin and his fellow travelers have at their disposal. A successor to Putin who could retain these tools would be difficult to unseat, even if the Putin mystique is nontransferable.
Policymakers in the United States and Europe must accept that Putin will persist in his war effort. A stymied economy and public skepticism are distractions from the essential story: that by now, the conditions that have made for an already long war are an organic part of Russia’s relationship to Europe, a shaping presence that will be exceptionally difficult, if not impossible, to eradicate. Putin has survived many crises: the wars in Chechnya in the late 1990s and first decade of this century; the 2000 sinking of the Kursk submarine (which made him look incompetent and helpless); multiple major terrorist attacks; the 2007–8 financial crash; and Prigozhin’s mutiny, among others. Arguably, most Russian elites have not obeyed the Kremlin out of deep loyalty or ideological alignment throughout Putin’s long reign. They have done so out of opportunism, and increasingly they obey out of fear.
Putin is prepared to prosecute this war for years to come, not because his advisers are promising him a quick victory, although they may be. The war is embedded in Putinism, just as Putinism is embedded in the war. His governing system gives him the freedom to do what he wants, and his legacy and the war are now inseparable. Both he and Russia are in it for the long haul.
articles.summary: Pressure and pain won’t sap Russia’s resolve in Ukraine.

articles.title: Europe’s Hidden Trade Advantage
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
JONAS NAHM is Andrew W. Mellon Associate Professor at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies.
The irony has not been lost on European policymakers. As U.S. President Donald Trump desperately casts about for a 51st state—Canada, Greenland, and Panama all said no this past year—the European Union’s membership queue is the longest it has been in decades. Despite the Trump administration’s accusations of civilizational decline in Europe, EU accession negotiations are advancing with an urgency not seen since the bloc’s last major expansion in 2004. Nine countries hold official EU candidate status, including Moldova, Montenegro, and Ukraine. Others are considering it, too. In a referendum in August, Iceland, which is already in the European Economic Area and enjoys many of the benefits of EU membership, narrowly voted not to reopen negotiations to join the bloc, 52.8 percent to 47.2 percent. Meanwhile, the United Kingdom, which left the European Union in 2020, is spending considerable political capital trying to rebuild the economic relationship it forfeited when it left.
Scores of other countries, meanwhile, are seeking closer economic ties with Brussels. The EU concluded trade negotiations with India and the South American trading bloc Mercosur in January, with Australia in March, and with Indonesia last September. This pace of new economic deals is unprecedented and partly a response to U.S. volatility. But it also reveals a rising global recognition that although the EU is relatively slow moving, the agreements it signs are dependable. Its bureaucratic process and institutional lethargy are proving, unexpectedly, to be an asset in an age of instability.
Trump came to office in January 2025 with a new theory of U.S. economic leverage. The United States is the world’s largest import market. Trading partners, he reasoned, needed access to U.S. consumers more than the United States needed access to their goods. That imbalance, if exploited with sufficient force, would produce concessions on trade flows, investment, and the rules governing global competition. His means of applying this force was tariffs, which were deployed at a speed and scale that rattled global markets.
Initially, it seemed that U.S. economic leverage had been judged correctly, since numerous framework agreements followed. But these were the product of executive actions—unratified by Congress and built on legal authorities that the courts were already contesting. When the Supreme Court ruled the tariffs unlawful in February, the administration replaced them with those empowered under a different statutory authority. Countries such as the United Kingdom, which had offered concessions to secure a deal, found themselves no more certain of the terms than before. It was becoming clear that U.S. trade policy could and would change overnight. The volatility that was supposed to generate leverage became instead a permanent condition, undermining the U.S. position.
Indeed, a year on, the results are not what the president predicted. The U.S. goods trade deficit reached a record $1.24 trillion in 2025, despite the highest effective tariff rate in generations. The deficit narrowed somewhat in the early months of 2026 but widened in July to $119.60 billion, 31 percent above the 12-month average. The tariffs did shift where Americans buy goods, and the deficit with China has fallen. But much of that trade was simply diverted rather than reduced—the three largest U.S. goods deficits are now with Mexico, Taiwan, and Vietnam.
The promised reshoring, meanwhile, has not arrived. Manufacturing shed tens of thousands of jobs through much of 2025, and although the sector has begun a modest recovery in 2026, total employment remains only marginally above where it stood when the tariffs took effect. Companies, it is now apparent, do not build factories on the basis of a 90-day tariff pause or a framework whose terms may not survive the next executive order. Again, the uncertainty that was supposed to generate leverage backfired. More than three-quarters of manufacturers surveyed through 2025 by the National Association of Manufacturers cited trade policy uncertainty as their top concern.
Trading partners have drawn their own conclusions. Canada, the United States’ largest trading partner, suspended trade negotiations in August after the administration introduced last-minute demands, which Prime Minister Mark Carney described as uneconomic and unfair. In explaining his decision to walk away, Carney said that the U.S. approach had “called into question the reliability of any deal.” Governments and investors must now permanently price in the risk of U.S. executive discretion. Regardless of who wins the presidency in 2028, formal trade agreements with the United States no longer offer any certainty that the specifics will remain unchanged over the medium term.
A growing number of countries, confronted by the uncertainty that this strategy has produced, have begun to look elsewhere. Their gaze is increasingly alighting on Europe, the world’s second-largest consumer market. For decades, the standard critique of the EU as an economic partner was that it was too slow, too rule-bound, and too hampered by the necessity of finding consensus among its 27 member states. That critique is not wrong. But the rules that complicate EU decision-making were designed to solve a specific and difficult problem: how to make economic integration possible across a continent of vastly unequal economies. The rules that slow the process also ensure that France and Germany cannot simply override the Netherlands or dictate terms to Portugal. That was the price the large economies paid to bring the small ones in. The rules of the single market—the level playing field, the shared external trade policy, and the jurisdiction of the European Court of Justice—were designed to make membership attractive to less powerful countries by guaranteeing that the more powerful ones could not call the shots. Nobody anticipated that these same rules would turn out to be an asset in a world shaped by volatility and executive authority.
The rules of the single market bind every member state equally. France cannot unilaterally grant its industries preferential treatment. Germany cannot override a common external trade policy because a new government finds it inconvenient. The constraints that frustrate European governments when they want to act quickly are the same constraints that make European commitments durable. No election can reverse them. No executive order can impose new terms overnight. An agreement concluded under Brussels’s rules, therefore, carries a different kind of assurance from one concluded under Washington’s. In the EU, trade agreements require negotiation by the European Commission, approval by a qualified majority of member states in the European Council, and, ultimately, the European Parliament’s consent before they fully enter into force. New defensive tariffs can be imposed only after the commission conducts a formal investigation, which is bound by statutory deadlines and triggered by evidence of injury to European industry. There is no equivalent in Brussels to such executive authorities as Section 301 or Section 232, which allow a U.S. president to impose or remove tariffs at will. The same logic that binds France and Germany internally also shapes how the EU engages externally: as a partner bound by rules rather than one that sets terms by power.
The United Kingdom tried a different approach. With leaders including then Prime Minister Boris Johnson arguing that a country of its size and trading relationships could do better outside European rules, the country voted to leave the EU in 2016. British business has since discovered that the rules that felt constraining turned out to be load bearing. The British government’s Office for Budget Responsibility has estimated that Brexit has reduced trade with Europe by 15 percent and made the economy four percent less productive—a loss of roughly $135 billion a year. A comprehensive U.S. free-trade deal, which leading advocates of Brexit argued was a certainty, never arrived. What came instead, in May 2025, was a four-page, nonbinding framework that reduced tariffs on a quota of British car exports and offered some relief on aerospace, subject to the same volatility that has defined U.S. trade policy. London is now going in a different direction, negotiating closer regulatory alignment with Brussels on agriculture, energy, and defense. These are modest steps toward rebuilding the economic relationship the United Kingdom walked away from.
When countries sign agreements with the EU, they are buying into a system whose core purpose is the preservation of rules and stability, one designed to outlast the political cycles of any member state. Access to the EU single market of 450 million consumers is valuable on its own terms. Less considered is the value of the institutional framework that comes with it. This economic power is not of a type that the EU set out to build, and as a consequence, it seems not to recognize what it has. This lack of awareness was on show in 2025, when, fearful of a trade war, Brussels squandered its own leverage and signed off on a lopsided framework with Washington. Under this agreement, the EU accepted 15 percent tariffs on most of its exports and pledged to make hundreds of billions of dollars in energy purchases and investment.
Attitudes may be changing. In February 2026, António Costa, president of the European Council, declared the single market to be Europe’s “superpower” and the EU “a trusted partner for those who want a reliable, predictable, and rules-based partnership in an increasingly challenging geopolitical environment.” Countries are drawing closer to the EU not only because of its market size but also because it offers terms that are durable. Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar put it plainly after signing the EU-Indian trade deal: “In a multipolar and uncertain world, the India-EU partnership will act as a factor of stability and resilience.”
Further proof is in the agreements themselves. The EU’s agreement with Mercosur, for instance, which took effect provisionally in May, was finally signed after more than 25 years of negotiations. It is the largest trade agreement Brussels has ever concluded, creating a trading zone of more than 700 million people across Europe and the four Mercosur economies of Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay. The EU was already the region’s largest foreign investor, with $453 billion invested across the four economies as of 2023. But annual trade between the two blocs—currently more than $125 billion—is projected to increase by 40 percent by 2040. The deal still requires the European Parliament’s consent and a Court of Justice review to enter into force. Unlike executive agreements that can be reversed overnight, EU trade commitments must run a gauntlet of institutional review before they become permanent. When Brazil ratified the agreement, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva described it not as a trade policy achievement but as a reaffirmation of multilateralism in an era of unilateral tariffs. “At a time when unilateralism isolates markets and protectionism inhibits global growth,” he declared, “two regions that share democratic values and a commitment to multilateralism choose a different path.”
Brussels also concluded an agreement with Indonesia, in September 2025, after nearly a decade of negotiations. This deal, covering Southeast Asia’s largest economy and 280 million people, eliminates tariffs on 98 percent of goods traded between the two. Crucially, Indonesia agreed to lift local content requirements in electric vehicle and renewable energy supply chains—a major concession from a country that had been using those requirements to attract manufacturing investment. EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic, when signing the agreement, described it as “a clear signal that the EU and Indonesia are choosing openness and partnership . . . in a world of rising protectionism.”
Brussels, perhaps realizing it has something of value to offer, has increased its ambitions since then. Its negotiations with Australia, which began in 2018 and concluded in March, paired a trade agreement with a security and defense partnership. The combination gives the EU preferential access to Australian lithium, manganese, and other critical minerals essential for electric vehicle batteries and renewable energy supply chains. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese described it as building resilience “in an increasingly uncertain global trade environment.”
The most ambitious of the recent agreements was finalized with New Delhi in January, concluding talks that began nearly two decades ago. This deal opens a market of nearly 1.5 billion people, growing at around seven percent annually, to Brussels’s exports. Indian tariffs on EU motor vehicles, previously over 100 percent, will fall to as low as ten percent. Duties on machinery, chemicals, and pharmaceuticals—currently as high as 44 percent—will largely disappear. Wine tariffs of 150 percent will be cut to between 20 and 30 percent. The agreement is projected to double EU exports to India by 2032. On services, the EU made its best-ever offer to any trading partner, opening 144 subsectors to Indian firms, and India reciprocated by opening 102 to European companies. A security and defense partnership was also signed alongside this economic package. India’s motivation was transparent: as U.S. tariffs on Indian goods reached 50 percent, New Delhi was looking to open new markets and reduce its vulnerability to Washington’s trade policy. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said that the deal “promises to create unprecedented opportunities and open new avenues of growth as well as cooperation.” Meanwhile, the EU, in the words of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, sought to “reduce strategic dependency at a time when global trade is being weaponized.” Both parties got what they were looking for.
Problems, of course, remain, and many European economies are struggling. Foreign direct investment in Europe fell seven percent in 2025, part of a broader global contraction driven by geopolitical uncertainty. Manufacturing’s share of EU GDP has fallen from 17 percent in 2000 to 14 percent today. The Industrial Accelerator Act, proposed in March, sets an ambition of raising that figure to 20 percent by 2035. But this target will require sustained political will across multiple election cycles, as well as institutional capacities that do not yet fully exist.
European economies are also threatened by a surge of Chinese exports, redirected to Europe partly by U.S. tariffs. French President Emmanuel Macron has described this flood of high-quality but affordable Chinese goods as a matter of life and death for European manufacturing. The EU finds itself simultaneously positioned as an attractive trading partner for countries reorganizing their economic relationships and as the destination for the overcapacity that the Chinese economic system generates and cannot absorb at home. Managing that tension—remaining open enough to be credible and protectionist enough to maintain the domestic political support for that openness—is the defining challenge of European industrial policy.
There is also a rising political risk inside Europe. The EU’s credibility as a trading partner depends on the durability of its institutional architecture—the single market rules, the jurisdiction of the European Court of Justice, and the common external trade policy. These are more resilient to a single election cycle than U.S. trade policy has proved to be. Changing the EU’s institutional architecture would require sustained political majorities across many member states over an extended period. Although that is a major challenge, the rise of parties skeptical of the integration project is not reassuring. The Alternative for Germany, or AfD, received more than 20 percent of the German vote in 2025, and France’s National Rally, although it has abandoned calls to leave the EU, now openly campaigns to assert national constitutional primacy over EU law and challenge Brussels’s regulatory authority from within. These parties’ platforms vary, but both point toward repatriating competences to national governments, weakening European Court of Justice jurisdiction, and loosening the common rules that make EU commitments credible to outside partners. Sustained across multiple member states over time, these attitudes could erode the institutional architecture that makes the EU such a valuable partner.
Finally, the European Union suffers from serious geopolitical vulnerabilities. A system requiring consensus among 27 member states is not built for rapid crisis response, and the bloc remains challenged by the lingering effects of the energy crisis, the shadow of Russian aggression, and internal divisions over wars in the Middle East. When events demand geopolitical agility, the EU’s institutional slowness is a liability, not an asset.
The conventional assumption has been that the fracturing of the U.S.-led order would produce a choice between two blocs—one organized around Washington, the other around Beijing. That may yet prove to be correct. But there is another possibility. Rather than seeing the emergence of a bloc, this would see the development of a network of overlapping bilateral, plurilateral, and interregional agreements that structure trade into long-term arrangements designed to bring down tariffs, embed supply chain relationships in legally binding frameworks, and extend the reach of common rules through market access rather than coercion. Brussels did not set out to build such a network. It has pursued agreements—with Australia, India, Indonesia, and Mercosur—for reasons specific to each relationship. But taken together, these agreements are beginning to amount to something larger. Washington is not excluded from this architecture. But a future U.S. administration that chooses to engage would be doing so on terms it did not write. That is not a position Washington is accustomed to.
If such a network proves durable, it would demonstrate that there is still a way of organizing the global economy that generates its own forms of reliability and trust, operating on different principles from those on offer in Beijing or Washington. The EU, long mocked for its institutional caution and complexity, turns out to possess precisely the kind of stability that this volatile moment demands. Brussels must recognize this strength and treat the durability of its institutional framework as a deliberate asset rather than an accidental feature. The implications extend beyond Brussels. Countries watching the current moment might conclude that executive agility and the willingness to weaponize economic relationships are the currencies of power in a volatile world. The EU’s experience suggests otherwise.
articles.summary: Slow and steady wins the negotiation.

articles.title: Iran’s Second Front
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
APRIL LONGLEY ALLEY is a Senior Fellow at the Washington Institute and served as Senior Political Adviser to the UN Special Envoy to Yemen from 2020 to 2024.
ALLISON MINOR is Director of the Project for Middle East Integration at the Atlantic Council and served as Deputy U.S. Special Envoy for Yemen from 2021 to 2023.
Seizing opportunity amid the war in Iran, the Houthis have launched a major new bid for military dominance in and around Yemen. On Tuesday, the Iranian-aligned group unleashed a wave of drones and ballistic missiles strikes on Saudi Arabia, setting fire to oil facilities in the country’s south and injuring more than 70 people. Then on Thursday, after days of heavy fighting along key frontlines inside Yemen, the Houthis routed Saudi-backed government forces along the Red Sea coast and captured the strategic port of Mokha. And on Friday, the Yemeni government reported that the Houthis had seized Perim Island at the mouth of the Bab el Mandeb Strait, the narrow waterway that connects the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean. The takeover marks a profound shift in the balance of power in Yemen, with potential consequences for the entire region.
Until this week, Mokha had been home to a vital part of the anti-Houthi coalition and served as a bulwark against the rebels’ advance. With this offensive, the Houthis have shattered a status quo along the coast, upended a truce that had largely held since 2022, and set the stage for further consolidation of their control of the north. But the victory is also Iran’s, since Houthi control of both Perim Island and Mokha, which lies less than 50 miles from the Bab el Mandeb, will allow the rebels to establish themselves as the power brokers of the strait and more easily harass shipping.
The timing of the Houthis’ escalation, which began with attacks on Saudi interests in July, is especially significant, given that the Red Sea has become a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz for Saudi oil during the Iran war. Even as Houthi leaders frame their actions in local terms, their alignment with Tehran appears to have tightened. By attacking Saudi shipping and Saudi Arabia itself, they have effectively opened a second front in the Iran war, broadening that conflict and placing further pressure on global energy and financial markets. Iranian officials have said that reaching a deal with the United States will require ending the blockade of Yemen—a shorthand for Saudi Arabia’s lifting all transit restrictions on Houthi-held territories, including the capital, Sanaa, and ending support for the Yemeni government. In this evolving regional order, Iran and its partners are trying to establish a new status quo by controlling the Middle East’s most critical maritime checkpoints.
Options for addressing the Houthi challenge are moving from bad to worse. While the frontlines will likely continue to evolve, a few hard realities have been laid bare. A decisive military solution to Houthi threats is not credible. For all their public bluster, Yemeni government forces remain internally fragmented. During this week’s offensive, their backer Saudi Arabia also failed to provide close air support and other necessary assistance, suggesting continued poor coordination between the anti-Houthi coalition and Riyadh. Moreover, the Houthis’ gains also undermine the prospects for a negotiated settlement. The militant group is now likely to be even more maximalist in its demands and in its ambitions to assert control across the Red Sea.
There are no easy solutions. For now, the priority for Saudi Arabia, the United States, and their Yemeni allies must be protecting other key frontlines from Houthi advances and hindering Houthi efforts to consolidate control over northern Yemen and the Bab el Mandeb. But beyond that, the anti-Houthi coalition must finally address the fissures that continue to tear it apart and agree on a credible political vision for resolving the Yemeni conflict. If it does not, there is a real risk of greater upheaval on the government side and expansion of the Houthi threat across the region.
For nearly five months after the Iran war began in late February, the Houthis mostly stayed on the sidelines. That relative calm gave way in mid-July, when the Iranians flew a Houthi delegation from Tehran to Sanaa, challenging the Yemeni government and Saudi-led coalition’s control of Yemen’s airspace. To prevent the aircraft from landing, Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government bombed the Sanaa airport’s sole runway. Although the plane landed at the Houthi-controlled port of Hodeidah instead, the Saudi action gave the Houthis a pretext for abandoning the 2022 truce. It was at that point that the group began their bold escalation against Saudi interests and launched their new offensive against coalition forces in Yemen.
The Houthi campaign is clearly designed to exploit new Saudi vulnerabilities. As Iran has throttled the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea has become a lifeline for the Saudi oil industry. But since the Houthis resumed their attacks in July, Saudi oil exports through the Bab el Mandeb have plummeted 95 percent. Now, by targeting infrastructure and ships near the Red Sea port complex of Yanbu, the Houthis are threatening the transit of oil exports northward through Egypt as well.
Meanwhile, the U.S. war with Iran has given new fuel to the Houthis’ maximalist goals in Yemen itself. The group became frustrated by the “no war, no peace” situation that prevailed after the truce, and they blame Riyadh for slow walking a formal political settlement to the 12-year-old civil war. In reality, such a deal was obstructed by the Houthis themselves. In 2023, the UN helped negotiate a road-map agreement that would have allowed the Houthis to pay all public-sector salaries and obtain a share of oil and gas resources in return for a permanent cease-fire and the launch of a political process. It would have been a good outcome for the Houthis, who control none of the country’s hydrocarbon resources and have been shut out of the international economy. But instead of taking the offer, they began attacking Red Sea shipping to show their support for Hamas in the Gaza war—all the while assuming they could return to the table when they were ready.
During the final phase of the war in Gaza, Israel and the United States caused significant military and economic damage to Houthi strongholds in Yemen. In the spring of 2025, the Trump administration undertook more than 1,000 airstrikes during Operation Rough Rider; a few months later, the Israelis targeted Houthi infrastructure and assassinated the group’s de facto prime minister and its military chief of staff. Yet these campaigns appear to have emboldened the group. By attacking global shipping, the Houthis bolstered their importance within Iran’s axis of resistance. And by engaging with these powerful militaries, the group reinforced its self-image as a major regional player that was uniquely capable of liberating the Muslim world from corrupting American and Israeli influence.
Since then, the organization has intensified its effort to acquire new and more powerful military capabilities. During the Gaza war, Russia had provided the Houthis with intelligence to assist its targeting of ships. It considered providing the Houthis with advanced weapons as well, although it was ultimately dissuaded by Riyadh. Today, as described in a recent analysis in Foreign Affairs, the Houthis are harnessing diversified supply chains and shadowy financial networks while building up domestic production capacity. As a result, they have been able to strengthen their arsenal—even without direct arms transfers from Iran.
Now the Houthis think they can get the Saudis to offer them even better terms than the 2023 UN-backed road map, including war reparations. As their military offensive progresses, those demands will likely continue to rise. The Houthis also face significant pressure at home to pay long-promised public-sector salaries and address increasingly desperate living conditions. More than half the population of Yemen is experiencing acute food insecurity, with six million people facing “emergency” levels of deprivation bordering on famine.
Given Saudi Arabia’s heightened dependence on the Red Sea, the Houthis may have calculated that the kingdom would quickly concede to their demands. Instead, Houthi actions seem to have steeled Riyadh’s resolve to confront the group. While Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman may have preferred de-escalation, or at least postponing a confrontation until a U.S.-Iranian deal reduced his kingdom’s dependence on the Red Sea, the Houthis have not given the Saudis leeway to wait.
With an unpredictable administration in Washington, Saudi Arabia has been preparing for confrontation by diversifying its security partnerships. On July 30, Riyadh announced a 14-country naval defense coalition for the Red Sea that included Turkey, Pakistan, Egypt, Sudan and Djibouti. A week later, the crown prince signed a mutual defense agreement with Turkey and Pakistan at a ceremony in Mecca with the leaders of both countries at his side. The military value of these accords is unknown, and indeed, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are a first test for the latter agreement. Thus far, the results have been lackluster. According to Reuters, Pakistan warned the Iranians to rein in their Houthi allies shortly before the Houthis’ dramatic takeover of Mokha. Neither Turkey nor Pakistan has directly entered the fight in Yemen, and Islamabad has confirmed that the Mecca accord has not been invoked in response to the Yemen war. Still, for Saudi Arabia, diplomatic support is important, given the criticism Riyadh faced over a military intervention in Yemen in 2015.
The Saudis have also continued to solicit support from the United States. Axios has reported that Washington gave Saudi Arabia the green light to strike the Sanaa airport, and the kingdom has asked for further U.S. support. On July 28, Riyadh teamed up with Washington to strike Iranian-backed Iraqi militias that have aligned themselves with the Houthis, a hint that Washington might join Riyadh in its military effort against the Houthis if the conflict continues to grow. Yet U.S. involvement is far from assured. Amid the demands of the Iran war, the administration has been keen to maintain a bilateral truce with the Houthis that has been in place since May 2025; many of its military assets in the Middle East are bogged down in the Strait of Hormuz, and expanding the war would be unpopular at home. While the Houthis’ seizure of Mokha and Perim Island puts greater pressure on Washington to respond, the Trump administration may be more concerned about avoiding new military entanglements ahead of the midterm elections: Axios reported that Trump declined Saudi requests to launch airstrikes against the Houthis after their advances on Thursday. Riyadh’s efforts to bolster the Yemeni government, meanwhile, have had decidedly mixed results. In January, Saudi Arabia pushed aside its longtime ally in Yemen, the United Arab Emirates, when UAE-aligned separatist forces led by the Southern Transition Council (STC) tried to assert control over all of south Yemen. Since then, the Emiratis have withdrawn from Yemen entirely, allowing Riyadh to unify government military forces under its direct command. But the Houthis’ rapid capture of Mokha raises large questions about the strength and cohesion of these forces. In battle, the unified command did not produce effective cooperation between different government-affiliated groups. As government troops from Mokha withdrew, there were even reports that they had clashed with southern forces who refused to let their northern allies enter the south with their weapons. In particular, the absence of the UAE and the dissolution of the STC have alienated an important southern constituency in the anti-Houthi coalition and deprived the coalition of a militarily capable external backer. If the Houthis are able to consolidate their gains in and around Mokha, the losses of territory could deal a powerful blow to morale among government-affiliated troops and stoke further division.
Iran’s greatest leverage against the United States has been its ability to shut the Strait of Hormuz. For much of the war, Saudi Arabia has been exporting three to five million barrels of oil per day via its Red Sea ports in what has become a crucial backstop for Riyadh and global oil markets. Through the Houthis, Iran can now restrict those exports as well. Tehran’s longer-term aim is to establish a daunting status quo: Houthi control over the Bab el Mandeb alongside Iranian control of Hormuz. If it could be sustained, such a strategy would make Iran and its regional partner de facto gatekeepers for trillions of dollars’ worth of trade each year.
Although Tehran does not exercise command and control over the Houthis, it exerts enormous influence on the group. Iran’s decision to send the flight to Sanaa in July, setting off the current Houthi escalation, suggests the many ways that Tehran can stoke the Yemen conflict for its own ends. In turn, the Houthis’ decision to enlist Iraqi militias in their attacks on Saudi Arabia has further entangled the Yemen conflict with the Iran war. The Houthis’ growing alliances with armed groups in Somalia, Sudan, and elsewhere across the Horn of Africa also suggest the extent to which their current escalation could quickly spill over into the broader region.
In the decade after Yemen’s civil war broke out in 2014, its effects reverberated into Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and finally the Red Sea. With the Iran war, the Houthis’ expanding regional ambitions and partnerships, and their combined ability with Iran to affect the global energy trade, the stage is now set for a more dangerous conflagration. This time, it could be much harder for the Houthis to preserve their earlier autonomy from Tehran. The war in Yemen has long been a battlefield for regional powers. But the latest stage could see expanding involvement from Israel, Russia, Turkey, and the United States. Rather than a battleground for regional influence, Yemen could become a platform for major-power competition centered on a critical maritime chokepoint.
Now that a dangerous cycle of escalation has started, much will hinge on what happens next. Saudi Arabia may use the recent Houthi advances to rally international support for a major campaign against the Houthis, potentially involving the United States and its new partners in the Mecca agreement. But such a response could expand the conflict without addressing the fundamental weaknesses of the anti-Houthi coalition fighting on the ground. Such an open-ended escalation is likely to favor the Houthis and further Iran’s strategy of controlling the Middle East’s chokepoints. A sustained Yemen war could also complicate U.S. efforts to reach a settlement with Iran. Alternatively, if the Saudis capitulate to the Houthis after their battlefield gains, it could deal a damning blow to the anti-Houthi coalition and further inflame Houthi regional ambitions.
Yet there is still a narrow window of opportunity to prevent uncontrolled escalation and return to the negotiating table. To do so, Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government—together with other regional and international partners—will need to agree on a credible plan for securing a political resolution to the Yemen conflict. The plan must address the divisions in the anti-Houthi coalition and settle the political questions that continue to tear that coalition apart while avoiding maximalist military objectives.
Getting to such a settlement now will require both Saudi Arabia and Yemeni government forces, with support of regional and international partners, to apply effective military pressure to stem the Houthis’ advances and persuade them to accept a deal. Indeed, the Houthis themselves are under considerable economic pressure at home and stand to benefit from such talks, if they can be convinced that they cannot impose their will militarily. For a political settlement to deliver stability in Yemen, the Houthis will also have to agree to terms that address core regional and Yemeni government concerns and set out a viable governance structure.
An earlier approach taken by the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen is instructive in this regard. In 2021, the Houthis walked away from negotiations and launched a major new ground offensive. The Saudis and Emiratis responded by mounting a coordinated operation that focused on getting the Houthis back to the table rather than aiming at total victory. Ultimately, the campaign helped bring about the truce months later. Any new campaign by the Saudi-led coalition today should be similarly focused on getting the Houthis to take part in negotiations. But success will first require preventing further losses on the ground and making an immediate effort to bridge divisions within the anti-Houthi coalition.
It is well past time to end the failed strategy of addressing Yemen’s problems through short-term military escalation and pressure campaigns. Reviving a political settlement will not be easy or happen immediately. But the alternative is far worse: stumbling into a renewed, protracted, and increasingly regional war that, as with the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran, could prove much easier to start than to end.

articles.title: The Other War on Terror
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
DANIEL BENJAMIN is President of the American Academy in Berlin. He served as Coordinator for Counterterrorism at the U.S. State Department from 2009 to 2012 and on the U.S. National Security Council from 1994 to 1999.
STEVEN N. SIMON is a Visiting Professor and Distinguished Fellow at Dartmouth College and a Senior Fellow at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft. He previously served on the U.S. National Security Council and in the U.S. State Department.
For years, the United States’ political dysfunction has been attributed to large-scale social and economic changes. Experts point to the failures of globalization, rising inequality, reduced social mobility, or the long aftermath of the “China shock” more than two decades ago to explain today’s extreme polarization, collapsing trust in institutions, democratic erosion, immigration backlash, and struggling middle class. Yet there is another widely overlooked factor that is equally central to understanding the United States’ current predicament: the war on terror.
Typically, when policymakers and analysts speak of the global war on terror—the defining fact of international affairs for two decades—they discuss the damage done to terrorist groups, the plots that have been thwarted, the rise and fall of jihadi ideology, the many intelligence failures, and, perhaps above all, the two forever wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. These are the scorecards of contemporary counterterrorism. But left out of this framing are the profound effects of this vast war on terror on domestic politics and society.
The human statistics alone tell an appalling story: more than 7,000 U.S. troops were killed in action, 53,000 were wounded, and well over 30,000 took their own lives—a staggering number. According to Brown University’s Costs of War Project, these conflicts added $8 trillion to the U.S. national debt, with trillions more projected in the future for veterans’ health care, including for the half million GIs with traumatic brain injuries and posttraumatic stress disorder.
Yet even these numbers fail to show the myriad ways in which two decades of war transformed the United States. For years, the fixation on Islamist terror shaped a culture drenched in fear, as voices from politics, the media, civil society, and a swelling counterterrorism-industrial complex insisted that the country faced an existential threat. Amid this climate, the government was given broad new powers to root out and prosecute potential jihadi activity wherever it might be, and the widespread assumption that there might be another terrorist attack began to reshape American society itself. Rather than bringing the country together behind a shared—and narrowly defined—enemy, however, the result has been a dramatic decline in social cohesion. It has contributed to the demise of political bipartisanship, already weakened in previous decades. At the same time, the war on terror fueled an alarming rise in xenophobia and anti-immigrant sentiment and discredited the country’s political and foreign policy elites.
Above all has been the uncontrolled expansion of executive power. This impetus did not begin with the war on terror; generations of American leaders and scholars have sought to increase presidential power, drawing up mechanisms that could sideline civil liberties and intertwine military and police activities. But after 9/11, these contingencies were used to give the executive branch sweeping new authority in the name of domestic security. And today, an authoritarian president is using these powers to target his political enemies. The United States, then, is overdue for a reckoning with the political legacy of the war on terror.
Anxiety about extended war has preoccupied American officials throughout U.S. history. In the first years after the country’s independence, James Madison, who would become the country’s fourth president, observed that “no nation can preserve its freedom in the midst of continual war.” More than a century and a half later, U.S. President Dwight Eisenhower sounded the alarm about “the acquisition of unwarranted influence” by what he famously called “the military-industrial complex.” As Eisenhower forewarned, “The potential for the disastrous rise of misplaced power exists and will persist.” For many of the decades since, much of that apprehension has been focused on the concentration of power in government and in the broader machinery of war. Yet during the war on terror, parts of society mobilized in parallel with the state and sought to cast a much wider net against a class of perceived enemies.
Terrorist acts are typically carried out by secret actors operating within a country’s borders, and 9/11 was the ultimate case in point. The attacks on the Twin Towers and the Pentagon—the first on U.S. soil since World War II—were carried out by foreign nationals inside the country. They were motivated by the al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden’s particular brand of jihadi ideology, which held that major attacks on the U.S. homeland would lead Washington to withdraw support for the apostate rulers of the Muslim world. These themes—which also carried notions of proportional revenge for the number of Muslims previously killed by the United States—and the attacks themselves gave license to Islamophobes throughout American society, including in the political world and policy establishment. The most influential came from the evangelical churches: to their huge audiences, leading televangelists such as Franklin Graham, John Hagee, and Robert Jeffress described Islam as “satanic” and a “heresy from the pit of hell” and its followers as a cult of pedophiles.
President George W. Bush sought to tamp down the hatred by insisting that the war on terror was not a war against Islam. But for all his protestations, many saw the war on terror as a crusade—a word that Bush himself used early on until he was told how poorly that played in the Islamic world. His message was further belied by such government actions as the detention of at least 1,200 Muslim men—many of whom were held on immigration charges but treated as high-security risks—and the severe curtailment of Muslim civil liberties by the FBI and other law enforcement in the name of addressing the terrorist threat. The fact that the 9/11 hijackers had been sustained by an efficient Muslim support network within the United States no doubt contributed to these measures, as did reasonable concerns about the potential for online radicalization.
In the decades since, the persistence of fear-mongering and the growth of anti-Muslim sentiment and hate crimes has been hard to miss. When the Obama administration sought to transfer foreign detainees captured in the war on terror from Guantánamo to facilities in the United States, Republicans depicted them as superhuman terrorists that no U.S. prison could safely secure. The plan was nixed. In 2014, when it was revealed that a jihadi’s laptop found in an Islamic State (ISIS) hideout in Idlib, Syria, contained some basic information on bioweapons, members of the flourishing counterterrorism commentariat claimed that terrorists planned to cull the African Ebola virus from victims’ corpses and spray it widely in American urban centers. Candidates for high office found the terrorist threat to be the gift that never ceased giving. Political scientists at Dartmouth, where both of us have taught, recall hearing former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, a candidate for the Republican presidential nomination in 2016, tell elderly women in a remote New Hampshire village that jihadis might take them hostage in their homes if they didn’t vote for the tough-on-terror candidate.
Claims such as these were contradicted by the actual state of the threat. By 2016, it had been several years since U.S. Navy SEALS had killed bin Laden, and al-Qaeda had not managed a second attack against the United States in 15 years. The few, ostensibly Islamist-related attacks that had happened on U.S. soil were mostly lone-wolf actions, in the sense that they were not deployed and directed by al-Qaeda operatives based outside the United States. Instead, they were radicalized in place through exposure to news reporting, online propaganda, preaching, and the fellowship of like-minded individuals. (A partial exception was the 2009 Fort Hood massacre, carried out by a U.S. army major, who had corresponded with Anwar al-Awlaki, the American cleric with links to al-Qaeda who was later killed by the United States in Yemen.) In 2014, ISIS captured global attention with its claim to a caliphate and insurgency in Iraq and Syria, and it was better than al-Qaeda at recruiting followers in Europe and North America. This group carried out or claimed responsibility for bloody attacks in Austria, Belgium, Finland, France, Germany, and Spain. Several of these were devastating mass casualty attacks, but none were in the league of 9/11. Notably, ISIS’s rise in the vacuum created by the U.S. toppling of Iraqi President Saddam Hussein was a result, not a cause, of the war on terror.
The lack of attacks was not simply luck. Throughout these decades, U.S. intelligence and law enforcement professionals—operating far from the overheated rhetoric of the era—dealt methodically and capably with the terrorist threat. During this period, government agencies achieved a level of integration that had improved dramatically since pre-9/11 days. Foreign intelligence services and civil authorities were tightly coordinated in the effort, making it possible to know who was attempting to cross the United States’ borders. Indeed, by the time al-Qaeda struck the United States again—a 2019 shooting at a Florida naval base that killed three and injured eight—the group was a shadow of its former self. As ISIS made clear, the fading of al-Qaeda did not usher in an age of Aquarius. Yet according to solid longitudinal polling, the degree to which Americans prioritized terrorism no longer reflected quotidian reality.
The unanswered and perhaps unanswerable question emerging from this period is whether the relative security Americans enjoyed in the decades after 9/11 owed more to intelligence and law enforcement and domestic security measures than to the progress of the expeditionary wars and targeted killings that were meant to root out the problem at its presumed source. Nonetheless, the question remains a vital one for those who are responsible for anticipating terrorism threats and constructing both defensive and offensive approaches to them.
In hindsight, 2016 marked a decisive hinge point in the war on terror, when the primary question shifted from faraway military conflicts to allegedly dangerous new threats at home—and not only those from Islamists. The United States had plenty of experience with nativism before 9/11. But a decade and a half of fear-mongering produced something entirely new. Perhaps nowhere was the legacy more pernicious than in the fusing of terrorist fears with broader anti-immigration sentiment. As numerous postmortems for the 2016 presidential election made clear, stoking anti-Muslim sentiment helped mobilize the Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump’s base, even though economic concerns won him that close election. On the campaign trail and then in office, Trump continually blurred the lines between Islamophobia and broader anti-immigrant sentiment. One day he decried murderers, criminals, and rapists coming across the southern border; the next, he asserted that the migrant flows were cover for jihadis.
Perhaps the perfect symbol of Trump’s fusion of the threat of terrorism with the challenge of illegal immigration was his repeated warnings in 2018 about a migrant caravan making its way from Central America to the U.S.-Mexican border—a caravan he claimed had “unknown Middle Easterners in it.” To be fair, the U.S. intelligence community was concerned that jihadis were exploiting chaotic conditions at the border to infiltrate the United States, but the fractured nature of interagency databases made this hard to know. In his effort to appear tougher than any competitor, Trump called for bringing back waterboarding and some unspecified technique that was “a helluva lot worse than waterboarding.” Speaking of ISIS operatives, he also said he would “take out their families.”
Still more striking, candidate Trump managed to radiate Islamophobia even as he decried the post-9/11 forever wars, stymieing his Republican rivals and his eventual Democratic opponent, Hillary Clinton. In a way, this marked a decisive shift in the war on terror toward the American homeland. One of the two candidates for president, one of the country’s foremost politicians, was expressly lumping together a sizable American ethnic minority with external enemies. Even when the subtext of previous policy suggested suspicion of American Muslims, federal leaders never expressed explicit hostility. Trump did. Once elected, he implemented a Muslim travel ban, which he introduced just a week into his term and reformulated repeatedly until the Supreme Court finally approved it 18 months later. He also created a permissive structure for xenophobes and racists, spurring a dramatic increase in hate crimes with victims from minority groups of all kinds and accelerating the disuniting of the United States.
In his second term, Trump has gone much further. In 2025, the administration invoked the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 against alleged members of the Venezuelan Tren de Aragua gang, described them as an invading force, and sent detainees to El Salvador’s Terrorism Confinement Center. The Supreme Court required adequate notice to permit habeas challenges, but removals had already begun. In Florida, the government opened a remote Everglades detention compound called “Alligator Alcatraz” that might usefully be thought of as Guantánamo transplanted to U.S. soil, with its geographic isolation and removal from the domain of law. The facility shuttered after a year, but only for reasons of expense; it cost over a billion dollars per year to run. And by then, the administration was making an even more direct connection with the war on terror, as some immigrant detainees were now sent to Guantánamo itself. The Pentagon also became involved, with active-duty personnel providing logistical and operational support for a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) detention mission. In other words, institutions created for external war, border enforcement, and domestic policing have now become components of a punitive system against immigrants who may not even have a criminal record. As a practical matter, it became a test bed for the detention of political prisoners, or, as Trump described them, “enemies of the people.”
The Trump administration is not alone in using Islamophobia to drive an anti-immigrant agenda. Texas Governor Greg Abbott, for instance, has long been famous for railing against illegal immigration. But as The New York Times put it in August, citing Republican consultants, “Islam has replaced the border as a major concern” for voters. To date, Texas officials have blocked a real estate development that includes a mosque and threatened to withhold state funding from airports that provide washing stations for Muslim prayer, among other steps. Meanwhile, Republican politicians across the country have denounced the electoral successes of Muslim politicians, including Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. Some have even suggested that these officials either are not American citizens or should lose their citizenship. Trump has remarked that “jihadists are being elected all over the place.”
The sociologist Charles Tilly’s maxim that “war makes the state; the state makes war” applies not just to early modern state formation but also to how the United States’ counterterrorism efforts led to a dramatic augmentation of state powers. The war on terror propelled the United States to collect and combine information, including on its own citizens; classify individuals it considered dangerous; combine both active and reserve component military units for the purposes of population control and law enforcement; and use coercive power under a variety of emergency authorities. It also reinforced an “us against them” conception of public life in which political disagreement could be recast as disloyalty and whole minority groups treated as presumptively suspect. The perception of an enduring terrorist threat increased support for coercive policies, even among Americans otherwise resistant to authoritarian appeals.
Of course, the United States faced security threats before 9/11. Yet whereas the Cold War security state depended on accurate intelligence on adversaries’ military forces and key assets, counterterrorism is focused not on large formations or fixed installations but on locating individuals hidden within large populations, both at home and in foreign societies. Defending against al-Qaeda required officials to identify suspicious people, trace money and travel, map personal networks, and act before an attack occurred. After the shock of the 9/11 attacks, Washington developed an information-sharing network that crossed the foreign and domestic divide and could search customs, immigration, intelligence, and regular law enforcement records. Joint Terrorism Task Forces set up by the FBI and state and city fusion centers created by DHS implemented this model in parallel at the local level. Their missions soon exceeded terrorism to encompass other facets of public safety. In time, national security institutions were routinely vacuuming up ordinary police information, and local law enforcement officers were combing through federal intelligence. The structure was built for finding needles in haystacks. Once built, it could search for needles of all sorts.
Such capabilities made it easy to expand political control and executive power, should an elected leader choose to use them for these purposes. Top government officials could identify not only suspects but also their associations, movements, communications, and supporters, making these tools convenient for targeting individuals and groups, both real and invented, and stigmatized communities. Commercial platforms increased their reach. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)—which was founded in response to September 11—has contracted with the American software company Palantir for ImmigrationOS, a system intended to assist in the selection and apprehension of deportation targets. Artificial intelligence, and its inherent scalability, has accelerated the process by eliminating the main bottleneck to comprehensive surveillance: scarce manpower. The logic was visible during the 2020 protests in Portland, Oregon, when DHS officers monitored social media, accessed travel and immigration records, and assembled dossiers on protesters and journalists. Unidentified armed federal officers used unmarked rental vehicles to detain people and took some to holding cells in the federal courthouse without explaining what agency held them or why.
The federal government’s evolution since 9/11 is reflected not just in its activities and capabilities. Its sheer mass has grown, as well. Since ICE was created in 2003, its annual budget has risen from $3.3 billion to almost $29 billion; in the same period, its corps of armed officers has grown from 3,000 to 22,000. Meanwhile, police forces across the country have transformed from lightly armed constabularies to small-scale armies. Before 9/11, the Defense Department had transferred only $27 million in hardware to local police forces. Since the attacks, the number has climbed to more than $1.6 billion. In numerous jurisdictions, police can now respond to demonstrations with mine-proof armored vehicles, camouflage, body armor, and large-caliber weaponry.
The government’s target set has also expanded. In 2025, the White House issued National Security Memorandum 7, which, among other things, designated antifa—a mostly made up, decentralized, left-wing political movement opposed to white supremacy and (per its name) fascism—as a domestic terrorist organization, a status not formally recognized in the law. The memorandum directed Joint Terrorism Task Forces to investigate organized political violence carried out by those who belong to this supposed network. The offenses were “anti-Americanism, anti-capitalism, and anti-Christianity . . . extremism on migration, race, and gender . . . hostility towards those who hold traditional American views on family, religion, and morality.” The crimes to be investigated by the task forces largely related to protected speech. A subsequent counterterrorism strategy document in May 2026 referred specifically to the “politically motivated killings of Christians and conservatives.” The document treats hostility to Christianity as one of the diagnostic markers for identifying organized political violence, alongside anticapitalism and anti-Americanism.
The Trump administration has also used counterterrorism precedents to justify the widespread use of lethal force. Beginning in 2025, the administration labeled suspected drug traffickers as narcoterrorists, giving it legal cover to use military strikes against boats and land sites in Latin America. By August 2026, its operations had killed hundreds of people, often without public evidence to establish a crime or even the basic identities of those targeted. Attacks against Iran in May 2026, meanwhile, killed much of the upper echelon of the Islamic Republic of Iran. Different legal authorities were invoked, but as with the purported drug dealers, the White House used classifications and military practices from the war-on-terror era to justify and conduct its operations. Although Israel’s preemptive and retaliatory reliance on targeted killings has drawn much attention, this mode of warfare characterized the American war on terror very nearly from its outset, including the arming of drones for this purpose; the first armed Predator flew in October 2001. During the Trump administration’s anti-immigration campaign within the United States, four Americans were killed and three wounded with the same impunity as the 526 targeted attacks conducted outside war zones from 2009 to 2016 during the latter phase of the war on terror. The war on terror’s focus on dangerous individuals, in other words, supplied a template that is now being applied to suspected criminals, foreign officials, heads of government, migrants, and protesters.
Domestic military deployment has followed a parallel track. In 2002, Washington established U.S. Northern Command to direct homeland defense and support civil authorities. In 2025, the army created Western Hemisphere Command by combining Forces Command, Army North, and Army South under one four-star headquarters responsible for readiness, homeland defense, and operations across the Americas. Neither change erased statutory barriers to domestic military law enforcement. But both reduced the organizational distance between military forces prepared for overseas combat and missions close to home. Since June 2025, the administration has deployed National Guard personnel or active-duty Marines to six American cities. It has also assigned active-duty personnel to support ICE processing and detention facilities. These steps did not formally merge the military and DHS, but they created recurring joint operations through which domestic coercive missions could expand.
Meanwhile, Trump is politicizing the armed forces, basing appointments and promotions on partisan loyalty and degrading or simply ignoring long-standing professional norms. These changes will presumably weaken the institutional barriers to the military’s political use, which concerns the missions the president assigned to military personnel, as in Los Angeles, where National Guard troops and Marines accompanied federal immigration operations. A federal district court found that troops had been systematically directed to perform law enforcement functions, including patrols and traffic control, in violation of the Posse Comitatus Act, and the administration ultimately halted these operations. But Trump has declared that they will resume on a larger scale. The homeland, he thinks, is an excellent place for U.S. armed forces to conduct battles. “We should use some of these dangerous cities as training grounds for our military,” Trump said in September 2025. “We’re under invasion from within. No different than a foreign enemy but more difficult in many ways because they don’t wear uniforms.” Urban opposition has been placed within a vocabulary of war.
War has not only changed the tenor of American life and enabled a vast expansion of executive power. It has also had a radicalizing effect on parts of the population, including war veterans—a phenomenon that bears echoes of the Freikorps, the groups of disbanded soldiers in Weimar Germany who, once given policing powers against the “Bolshevik” threat, quickly became a lethal paramilitary force. In her history of the white power movement, the scholar Kathleen Belew has shown how a segment of Vietnam veterans joined civilians in building a narrative of betrayal, transferring military skills and organizational forms into paramilitary politics to be redirected against enemies at home. The 1992 Ruby Ridge confrontation and the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing came from that milieu.
Today, a recurrence of that pattern can be seen among veterans of Afghanistan and Iraq. Groups such as the Oath Keepers and the Three Percenters recruit current and former military personnel and police officers. Its members used military formations during the January 6 attack, and the founder of the Oath Keepers was convicted of seditious conspiracy. Of these, all had their cases dismissed, were pardoned, or had their sentences commuted by Trump. How dangerous these groups still might be is poorly understood: the Trump administration has banned contact between scholars and military personnel except in the framework of professional military education, so there is no up-to-date survey data or qualitative information on attitudes within the military about political matters. Publicly available government reporting on militias has also dried up. Given that such groups have had practical and rhetorical support from the administration in power, the threat of more violence cannot be discounted.
