articles.title: The Coming Risks to Russian Power
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
ANDREY KORTUNOV is a Moscow-based analyst with experience working for Russia’s Academy of Sciences, leading international think tanks, and research universities. This essay emerged from the Lloyd George Study Group on Global Governance.
The United States has long viewed Russia as a power in terminal decline. This assessment formed in the 1980s as the Soviet Union began showing clear signs of imperial overstretch, and it congealed after the collapse of first the Warsaw Pact and then the Soviet Union itself. Washington went on to pursue a policy agenda, including NATO enlargement, that treated Russian power and interests as an afterthought, and the long-standing conflict over Ukraine turned dismissiveness into condescension. In March 2014, U.S. President Barack Obama called Russia “a regional power” that was “threatening some of its immediate neighbors, not out of strength but out of weakness.” President Donald Trump shows more fondness for Russian President Vladimir Putin than his predecessors did, but most Russia watchers in the West still dwell on Russia’s lagging technology; its failure to rescue allies in Syria, Venezuela, and Cuba; and what they see as its reduction to a vassal of mighty China.
This picture of Russia as feeble and fading may suit the biases of Putin’s many critics, but it is fundamentally at odds with reality: Moscow consistently punches above its weight in global affairs. Thirty-five years after the disintegration of the Soviet Union, Russia remains a nuclear superpower. As during the Cold War, NATO treats it as the benchmark threat around which the alliance plans its forces. An unprecedented wall of Western sanctions has failed to trigger the economic collapse its architects predicted or to erode political and social stability. The effort to isolate Moscow has faltered as well. The Kremlin has skillfully promoted non-Western bodies such as BRICS, a grouping of major emerging economies, and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, a Eurasian political and security group. In so doing, it has extended its influence over the post-Western order now taking shape. And even though Russia’s economy is far smaller than China’s, the “no limits” partnership between Moscow and Beijing has produced a formidable coalition.
This bullish assessment comes with a caveat: it relies on the international conditions that prevail today. Moscow continues to punch above its weight because it is navigating a fragmented, unpredictable world that plays to its strengths. Volatility and instability, active conflicts and arms races across several regions, economic decoupling and the retreat of globalization, the worldwide rise of nationalism and populism, the discounting of soft power and fissures in the Western alliance—all these features of the existing international order work to Moscow’s advantage.
The downside risk for Russia is that today’s turmoil and uncertainty may not last. The pendulum is likely to swing back, with global disorder subsiding and the international system consolidating anew. That reversal could come when Trump leaves the White House, especially if his successor restores traditional U.S. support for the transatlantic alliance, multilateralism, and open trade. A planetary shock—accelerating climate change, an out-of-control AI system, or some other surprise—could likewise push states to set aside their current conflicts in favor of closer cooperation. When this change happens—and it will—Russia may find that its time-tested foreign policy and its once reliable but rigid institutions no longer serve it well.
The centrifugal trends pulling the international system apart work to Moscow’s advantage. In a fragmented and dangerous world of strongmen, where raw power decides outcomes, Russia’s military heft remains a durable source of strength and influence. Russia is also the only power that can rival the United States in strategic nuclear weapons. China is modernizing and expanding its arsenal, but Beijing will need a long time to catch up with the two superpowers. Russia’s nuclear status has practical effects: it has deterred NATO members from deploying troops to Ukraine, and it gives Moscow powerful diplomatic leverage on arms control, strategic stability and risk reduction, nonproliferation, and the prevention of nuclear terrorism.
As for its conventional capabilities, Russia retains a blue-water navy and long-range strike capabilities; only the United States can project power more widely. To be sure, the initial phase of fighting in Ukraine in February 2022 exposed serious weaknesses in the Russian army. But over the four and a half years since, the armed forces have transformed themselves, sharply improving their efficiency and combat power. Moscow now fields one of the world’s strongest militaries and, beyond that, has unique experience in next-generation ground warfare—an edge over almost any other fighting force, the United States included. Ukraine, too, has adapted its forces and tactics to new battle technologies, but it depends on Western support and may not be able to preserve those capabilities once the fighting stops. The accumulated experience of Russia’s armed forces will keep serving Moscow well in an era of frequent conventional wars.
A divided, resource-scarce world also magnifies the leverage that Russia’s vast natural endowments give it. Russia is a supplier of oil, natural gas, coal, wheat, fertilizers, uranium, critical metals, diamonds, and other commodities. It regularly plays the role of dealmaker, especially now that supply, not price, is the priority. Europe, for instance, may be weaning itself off Russian fossil fuels, but China’s reliance on those supplies helps offset the asymmetries in the relationship between Moscow and Beijing. The vulnerability of Middle Eastern supply routes during the Iran war has further strengthened Russia’s hand.
A fiercely competitive, volatile environment also raises the value of Russia’s centralized economic and political systems. In the West, these are often derided as antiquated, inflexible, and harmful to the country’s development. Yet a strong state has helped Russia maintain social, economic, and political stability despite Western pressure and its losses in Ukraine. In an era of heightened polarization, Russia’s centralized, personalized decision-making carries clear advantages over the liberal alternative. Putin governs with little opposition, few divisions within the establishment, and scant pushback from the media, and he can pursue the kind of long-term strategic planning that unpredictable election cycles in the West rule out.
The United States, meanwhile, is a divided political mess, presided over by a mercurial president and a dysfunctional Congress. Trump seems not only to respect Putin but also to envy him and his tight grip on Russia. In Britain and France, prime ministers come and go, none able to sustain public confidence. The European Union survives for now, but it makes decisions with excruciating slowness and, within its member states, faces surging support for populist parties eager to topple the bureaucrats in Brussels.
As long as the international system favors rivalry over cooperation, security over prosperity, regionalization over globalization, and sovereignty over interdependence, Russia will remain in the top tier of global politics. It will even hold comparative advantages over countries with far greater commercial, financial, and technological capacities. Its rivals will be constrained by their own democratic gridlock and restless electorates. Russia cannot beat the West outright, but it can hold its own and play for a draw—until, that is, today’s competitive and fragmented order gives way to compromise, de-escalation, and stability.
History moves in cycles, and the current configuration of the international system could prove fleeting. Globalization could return in a new form, and instability could give way to a long stretch of stable peace. The seemingly endless fighting in the Middle East could finally stop; Washington and Beijing might reach a sustainable trade and geopolitical compromise; the European Union may overcome its existential crisis; and a new UN secretary-general could succeed in reviving principles of multilateralism in global affairs. The reversal of the pendulum could begin as early as the coming midterm elections in the United States, if they result in a major defeat for Trump’s supporters on Capitol Hill.
In such a world, some of the foreign policy assets Russia now prizes most would begin to lose their value. The softer forms of power, which Russia has long underrated, would matter more. Heavy investment in strategic and conventional forces, for instance, gives Moscow geopolitical heft, but it does nothing to help Russia plug into emerging high-value global supply chains. Were its domestic market as vast as China’s or India’s, Russia could insulate itself from the risks associated with globalization’s return. But its long-term demographic decline forecloses that option. Exporting its way out of hardship by selling even more hydrocarbons won’t work either, given the likely fall in demand for fossil fuels. Competing for large-scale foreign direct investment would be harder still. It requires high levels of interstate trust and transparency, as well as a stable and user-friendly legal framework.
The country’s geography offers some advantage. With the world’s longest Arctic coastline, Russia can command a large share of the High North’s resource reserves and of the new shipping routes that will open as the climate warms. But to capitalize on its position as a transit corridor between East Asia and Western Europe, Russia would need long-term, stable partnerships with not only China but also the EU. Such relationships are hard to imagine now.
Finally, without a strong civilian high-tech ecosystem, Russia could find itself far behind the United States and China in technological prowess. For over two decades, Russia’s leadership has been tightening its grip on the private sector. Its highly centralized decision-making has helped the Kremlin mobilize resources quickly and head off political and social developments that threaten the state, but it has also suffocated the entrepreneurial energy the country needs to regain its technological edge and compete in the marketplace of tomorrow. Russia’s innovation infrastructure remains rooted in the twentieth-century Soviet state-centered model. But today’s technological transformations—AI and robotics, clean energy, quantum computing, gene editing—demand new modes of interaction between states and private businesses, from global platforms down to the garage startups that often lead in key breakthroughs.
How Russia fares over the long run will depend on its ability to hedge against and prepare for another change in the world order. Its current “besieged fortress” model treats the international environment as a challenge rather than an opportunity. It can minimize immediate external risks, but it also keeps Russia from making full use of its geography, resources, and human capital. Perpetual confrontation with the United States and Europe does not serve Russia’s long-term development. The West may keep declining in power, but it will remain indispensable to Russia’s external environment—sometimes a problem for Moscow, sometimes part of the solution. Peaceful coexistence, and even limited cooperation, is the better path.
Restoring ties with the EU matters most of all. These days, it is easy to forget that its member states were once Moscow’s main economic partners and its chief source of new technology and modern business practices. Given the dismal state of Russian-European relations, even a partial rapprochement will take considerable time. Once the conflict in Ukraine ends, however, the two sides could begin the slow work of repair.
It is also in Russia’s own interest to do its part to uphold international legal norms, especially those coming from the United Nations and other global bodies, even when that means making concessions and giving up potential short-term gains. To be sure, a world governed by “might makes right” offers Moscow real opportunities in the short run. But over the long run, it is a dangerous game. The international balance of power is swiftly shifting, and new actors are rising. A strong international legal system—backed by all major powers, including Russia—may prove one of the few safeguards against revisionist temptations.
Russia is, to the dismay of its critics, holding strong and proving itself in the current moment. But to sustain that success, it will have to look beyond short-term gains and narrow self-interest. It must be able to withstand upheaval in the international system and rapid technological change. Russia has the resources and wherewithal to determine its own course, but it is clinging too tightly to its preference for stability over change. This is understandable, given the painful memories of the 1990s, when change came as catastrophe, costing millions of Russians not just their jobs and savings but self-respect, belonging, even a reason to live. But that preference can also harden into a refusal to adapt—a calcification that has pushed great powers to the sidelines before.

articles.title: The Case for Letting China In
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
BRIAN DEESE is an Innovation Fellow at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. He served as Director of the National Economic Council from 2021 to 2023.
Industrial policy is back in fashion in the United States. As fragile global supply chains and a weakened industrial base present growing economic and national security risks, policymakers in both parties have embraced energetic efforts to rebuild the country’s industrial capacity. With interventions such as the 2022 CHIPS and Science Act, Washington has made historic commitments to strengthening the United States’ technology and manufacturing base, which is becoming increasingly important to the country’s economic success and ability to defend itself. As director of U.S. President Joe Biden’s National Economic Council, I helped to design and drive this shift.
Initiatives to revive domestic capacity are a necessary response to real dangers. But more and more, American leaders are seeking to support industry at home in ways that are counterproductive. In particular, they are growing hostile to foreign investment.
Many policymakers fear that foreign investors could steal sensitive data or gain dangerous leverage over U.S. companies or critical infrastructure. Their aversion is most pronounced with respect to China but has been trained on allies and partners as well. It applies not only to cases of foreign ownership of U.S. companies but also to joint ventures, the licensing of foreign intellectual property, and other arrangements in which a foreign company shares its knowledge or resources. Stephen Miran, the chair of the president’s Council of Economic Advisers, has suggested imposing fees on foreign holdings of U.S. assets, including those owned by allies. Senators Tammy Baldwin and Josh Hawley have introduced bipartisan legislation in the U.S. Congress that would tax foreign capital inflows outright.
At the federal, state, and local level, those in power are taking steps to shut global capital out of the United States and prevent American enterprises from harnessing the latest advances in data storage, critical mineral processing, and chip-making. This is a troubling and ultimately self-defeating strategy. Of course, the U.S. government should mitigate the risks of foreign investment. But today, its screening regime is overzealous. The United States is undermining its own industrial policy by denying itself the tools to become competitive globally in crucial sectors.
What the country needs is a new framework for selectively encouraging investment from abroad to match its industrial ambitions. The U.S. government’s existing policy toolkit isn’t designed to take on this task. Washington has an elaborate apparatus for saying no to inbound investment but few ways of getting to yes. An improved system would welcome foreign capital and know-how while maintaining transparency, protecting U.S. data, and ensuring that Americans have control of companies when it matters. The fact is, the frontier of knowledge for many industries lies outside the United States. The federal government must get better at weighing the risks and rewards of foreign investment to take advantage of that expertise.
Throughout its history, the United States has used foreign knowledge and tools for its own gain. At the turn of the nineteenth century, for example, the country’s military readiness depended on a fledgling domestic gunpowder industry. Washington could no longer rely on its single foreign supplier, Britain, against which it had just fought a revolution. Supported by a significant French investment, the chemist Éleuthère Irénée du Pont brought French expertise in advanced manufacturing techniques to the United States, establishing a company in 1802 that would quickly become the biggest purveyor of explosives to the U.S. government. The firm, DuPont, remained at the center of innovation in U.S. chemical and materials production for centuries.
Foreign knowledge has proved invaluable in more recent cases, too. In the early 1980s, when U.S. car companies were lagging behind their Japanese competitors, General Motors and Toyota jointly reopened a shuttered GM plant in Fremont, California. By bringing in state-of-the-art Japanese manufacturing systems, the companies transformed a failed factory into the most productive auto assembly plant in the United States within two years—while largely retaining the same American workforce. The methods GM picked up from Toyota are now standard across U.S. auto manufacturing.
The CHIPS and Science Act was designed to replicate these and other successes, but with semiconductors. American lawmakers understood that creating a domestic chips industry would require investment and expertise from companies such as South Korea’s Samsung and the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. Under the 2022 law, Washington issued grants and loan guarantees to firms, domestic and foreign, to build semiconductor fabrication plants in the United States and to train American workers in chip making, which is notoriously difficult to master. The act also funded the National Semiconductor Technology Center, which facilitates technology transfers and shared research and development between domestic chipmakers and foreign ones operating in the United States. Companies that accepted money from the U.S. government were barred from expanding advanced chip capacity in China.
If efforts to encourage foreign investment from U.S. allies and partners have proved contentious at times, deciding how to treat investment from the United States’ biggest rival, China, has been downright incendiary. More than any other government in history, Beijing has aggressively wielded the tools of economic statecraft. Its theft of intellectual property and enormous subsidization of domestic industry, combined with Washington’s longtime complacency, have hollowed out manufacturing capacity in much of the world and created dependencies on China for many critical technologies. It is easy in this context to conclude that the United States must keep out Chinese investment. The analyst Oren Cass, for instance, recently argued that allowing Chinese companies to invest in the United States would be “an unforced error of world-historic proportions” because it would cede dangerous economic influence to Beijing.
But if the United States wants to produce more advanced goods, it needs to remain open to foreign investment, including from China. Indeed, China itself followed the same playbook beginning in the 1980s, luring U.S. companies to its shores with cheap labor, low taxes, and access to its vast domestic market. Much of China’s expertise can be linked back to foreign companies that set up factories in the country—expertise that Chinese firms later used to outcompete their foreign counterparts. In 2018, for example, China convinced Tesla to establish manufacturing facilities in Shanghai by offering cheap land, low-interest state loans, tax breaks, and permission to fully own its plant. Chinese automakers absorbed what they needed from Tesla and applied those lessons to propel the domestic electric vehicle sector forward.
China is now at the forefront of many critical technologies, including electric vehicles and energy storage. Gaining access to that knowledge via foreign investment is, in many cases, the only way for the United States to catch up.
Chinese companies are already doing business in the United States in limited cases. In 2023, Ford announced a multibillion dollar plant in Marshall, Michigan, that will manufacture batteries for electric cars with technology and know-how licensed from China’s largest battery maker, CATL. Ford fully owns the facility but has a long-term agreement that enables it to train its workers on CATL’s core technological processes. Eventually, Ford could use the expertise learned from CATL to design and produce its own batteries without Chinese licenses.
What Ford is doing in Michigan provides a model for an ambitious industrial strategy: encourage investment, work with foreign firms when necessary, and learn by doing. The partnership was possible because of a novel intellectual property-sharing arrangement with CATL that entailed licensing but not foreign ownership of the facility. In many other cases, however, presidential directives and onerous regulations get in the way of deals that have similar potential to strengthen the U.S. industrial base. U.S. presidents from both parties have used their authority under the Defense Production Act to block major foreign direct investments out of fear that sensitive American technology and data will fall into the wrong hands. The Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS), the government body that reviews deals that could threaten national security, has become backlogged, difficult to navigate, and overly cautious. When the committee identifies a concern with a foreign company’s proposed investment, the firms involved frequently cannot negotiate a resolution within the statutory deadline and end up starting the process from the beginning. In 2024, applicants withdrew and refiled nearly a quarter of all notices. Filings have declined because the lengthy process discourages companies from even trying.
In other cases, the problem is a lack of regulation altogether. CFIUS, for example, generally screens only those transactions in which foreign entities seek to acquire an interest in an American business. If a foreign company, say, wants to license out the use of its equipment, there is no formal review process through which it can receive approval. Such an arrangement falls into a gray zone, vulnerable to a political attack. Congress spent years threatening to disqualify Ford’s electric vehicle plant in Michigan from receiving a tax credit and investigated it for national security risks, in part, because the plant was not subject to any review process.
To encourage American companies to pursue strategic foreign partnerships, the U.S. government must cut red tape and stop reflexively rejecting investment. It should treat capital from close allies as different from capital from countries of concern such as China, Iran, and Russia. It should also develop new systems to review and greenlight new models of foreign investment and partnership.
When it comes to allies and partners, CFIUS should simplify its process. To reduce the number of U.S. companies and foreign investors that need to apply for approval, it ought to expand its list of countries whose firms are exempt from this requirement—currently just Australia, Canada, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom—to include Japan, South Korea, and countries in Europe. Low-risk deals, such as investments in software companies whose only critical technology is routine encryption, should be exempt from filing, and there should be more rapid approval for pre-vetted investors.
Most important, CFIUS should change how it judges the deals it does review. It should, for instance, analyze transactions on the basis of whether a foreign adversary could plausibly exploit the investment to harm the United States, instead of fixating on the investor’s nationality and business affiliations. The committee must also change its risk calculus. Today, the body can approve foreign investments in U.S. companies only by certifying that there are no unresolved security concerns. That means even a deal that would benefit national security overall cannot be approved if doubts linger about any single component of the arrangement. If resolving those doubts is impractical, the deal dies altogether. In other words, CFIUS only takes risk into account, not opportunity. Congress should replace this standard with one that lets the committee approve investment deals that are, on balance, in the national security interest.
For more risky investments, such as those by Chinese companies, the U.S. government should adopt a model similar to the Defense Department’s Foreign Ownership, Control, or Influence program, which polices foreign control over defense contractors. The framework allows critical U.S. industries to benefit from foreign investment while guarding against foreign access to American secrets and foreign influence over key industries. Consider BAE Systems. The defense firm is wholly owned by a British parent company, yet it employs roughly 35,000 Americans, generates close to $13.6 billion in annual sales, is among the Pentagon’s largest suppliers, and is deeply involved in classified projects. This arrangement is possible because, under FOCI, a special agreement restricts the parent entity’s control over BAE Systems. The company has a separate U.S. board dominated by American directors with security clearances, and firewalls shielding technology, products, and programs from the foreign parent company. The arrangement gives the United States another major contractor competing for Pentagon work, tens of thousands of domestic manufacturing jobs, and access to British technology and capital. The British parent company, for its part, gets to profit from the world’s largest defense market. Meanwhile, the risk of leaks remains relatively low.
Today, the FOCI regime applies only to companies that do business with the U.S. government on classified contracts. A system based on this program, however, should also be used to assess the risk and opportunity of foreign investments in companies that don’t need security clearances but could pose national security risks, such as those that make advanced chips, batteries, drones, or critical software. The Department of Commerce, which has already started negotiating arrangements with semiconductor companies that resemble those the Pentagon reaches with defense contractors under FOCI, could oversee an expanded system immediately under existing authorities (some of which were granted by the CHIPS Act). But Congress should codify the department’s authority to review and request adjustments to deals involving foreign adversaries. In practice, a firm contemplating an acquisition, joint venture, or licensing arrangement would submit a proposal to the Department of Commerce, which could add safeguards to the deal before issuing its approval.
The goal is to give American companies more options for entering partnerships with foreign firms, with safety measures tuned to the specific risk presented by the investment. When the risk is that sensitive information may be leaked, a new FOCI-based system might allow foreign ownership as long as the parent company’s access to sensitive technology, data, and day-to-day decisions is severed through proxy boards, security agreements, and cleared American directors. When the foreign firm holds expertise the United States needs but is based in China or another country of concern, the right template may look like the Ford plant in Michigan, where an American company retains operating control but benefits from foreign ingenuity. Under such a system, the government would no longer default to rejecting deals but act as a creative problem solver.
Establishing new pathways to approve foreign investment will not be easy. The politics of blocking these transactions are well entrenched in both parties. Regulators are so afraid of approving a deal that leaks sensitive technology or hands adversaries control over a key company that they err on the side of restricting access to knowledge, money, and production capability from abroad.
The way to calm those fears and bring in productive foreign investment is to execute foreign deals competently. The Trump administration has treated announcements of major foreign investments as ends unto themselves but has shown little appetite for building a process to encourage safe deals with foreign companies. Democrats should embrace openness to foreign investment but improve on the practical application of that philosophy by championing legislation that institutionalizes a better and more transparent method for vetting agreements. With a system that approves the right kind of partnerships, the United States can gain the experience it desperately needs to revitalize its industrial capacity. From du Pont’s gunpowder to Arizona’s semiconductor factories, the United States has always become stronger not by walling itself off from the world’s know-how, but by making that knowledge its own.
articles.summary: American businesses need more foreign capital and know-how.

articles.title: The Right Way to Sanction Russia
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
ROBIN BROOKS is a Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution.
BEN HARRIS is Vice President and Director of Economic Studies at the Brookings Institution. He was Assistant Secretary for Economic Policy in the U.S. Treasury Department from 2021 to 2023.
When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, Western countries responded with aggressive economic restrictions, freezing Russia’s official foreign exchange reserves, placing export controls on critical technology, and sanctioning scores of its political, military and business leaders. Yet more than four years later, the war is still going on, and Western sanctions have inflicted only limited pain on the Russian economy. Russia continues to trade oil and other commodities, recently receiving a massive windfall as the closing of the Strait of Hormuz caused global oil prices to soar. These profits are raising the government’s tax revenue at a critical time, helping it fund the war in Ukraine and stabilize the country’s financial markets. If sanctions were looking ineffective before, Russia’s economic rebound since the start of the United States’ and Israel’s war with Iran have only strengthened that perception.
But it is wrong to write off sanctions as a policy tool. When Western policymakers portray them as a wasted effort or counterproductive, their governments are playing right into Moscow’s hands. And they are discounting the enormous strain that sanctions could still place on the Russian system if properly enforced. By reducing the flow of hard currency into Russia, sanctions have the potential to send the ruble into a spiral of depreciation, which in turn would send inflation soaring and destabilize the country’s broader economy.
It is not too late to make sanctions effective. One-fifth of Russia’s GDP is directly linked to oil and gas extraction, and exports account for nearly one-third of government revenues. Russia evades Western oil sanctions primarily by using a shadow fleet of oil tankers, and that fleet is vulnerable to European pressure. It passes through European-controlled waterways, replenishes its numbers with European-owned ships, and can be forced to engage with a Western-dominated insurance industry. All of this gives Europe the power to restrict the fleet’s operations, and thereby drastically reduce Moscow’s ability to finance its ruinous war.
The sanctions that the United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom, and Canada placed on Russia in early 2022 ran the gamut. They included export controls on sensitive goods such as semiconductors, computers, and lasers as well as the freezing of Russian foreign exchange reserves held by Western central banks. Yet efforts to curtail Russia’s oil exports back then were limited. The world economy was still rebounding from the COVID-19 pandemic, oil demand was strong and rising, and Russian oil accounted for roughly one-tenth of global supply. Western countries did not want to drive up prices by embargoing Russian oil, but the mere fear that they might do so caused oil prices to surge anyway, delivering enormous profits to Moscow. Russia’s current account surplus, or the amount by which its export receipts exceeded its import payments, soared to an all-time high of $235 billion in 2022. Within one year, Russia had nearly recouped the foreign exchange reserves that were frozen by Western countries.
Western countries needed to figure out a way to prevent Moscow from generating large amounts of cash from oil exports without causing global prices to spike. Many oil and commodity analysts worried that any attempt to take Russian oil off global markets could lift crude prices from their prewar baseline of around $75 per barrel to $200 or higher, allowing Russia to make enormous profits from its remaining exports even if the volume of exports were lower. Such a substantial price increase would almost certainly drive the world into recession.
The solution the G-7 came up with in December 2022 was an oil price cap. Around 70 percent of the vessels shipping Russian oil were Western-owned and close to 90 percent used Western insurance, financing, and brokering services. G-7 members, Australia, and the EU agreed to allow Russian exporters to use those services—but only if the crude oil they were selling was priced below $60 per barrel. There were also separate price ceilings for high-value refined products, such as diesel, and low-value refined products, such as naphtha, which is used in refining and in the production of plastics. The idea was to set the caps high enough that Russia would continue to export oil but low enough to constrain its revenue.
Together with a European ban on purchasing any seaborne Russian oil regardless of price, the cap immediately reoriented the global oil trade. Suddenly, Russia was selling most of its crude oil to Asian markets, especially China and India, where buyers were able to negotiate prices well below those of Western grades. By January 2023, Russian crude was selling for almost 40 percent less than the global benchmark, depriving Russia of billions in profits each month. The country’s current account surplus began to decline, falling to $50 billion in 2023 and bouncing back only slightly to $63 billion in 2024.
Yet Russia found ways around the cap as time wore on. Because enforcement depended on Western ownership of the vessels shipping Russian oil, Russia could evade the restrictions by loading crude exports onto ships flying third-country flags but controlled, through a labyrinth of shell and holding companies, by Moscow. By 2023, the shadow fleet was expanding by about seven oil tankers per month. Around half the ships were purchased from Western owners, most of them based in Greece. The EU attempted to block such transfers in a December 2023 sanctions package, but the sales continued, although they are now routed through shell companies before reaching Russia.
Western countries eventually cracked down on the shadow fleet, sanctioning large numbers of vessels known to carry Russian oil subject to the price cap. The United States led the way, placing almost 200 ships on its sanctions list in the final days of the Biden administration, and the EU and the United Kingdom followed suit soon after. When a tanker is on Washington’s sanctions list, in particular, any entity that does business with it risks exclusion from the U.S. dollar payment system. Losing access to that system would be so debilitating that the mere threat of these secondary sanctions is enough to deter most companies from doing business with sanctioned entities.
Yet this success proved short-lived. The United States stopped sanctioning additional ships under President Donald Trump, even as the EU’s and the United Kingdom’s sanctions lists grew to more than 600 vessels. Without the threat of U.S. secondary sanctions, the 524 vessels that currently are subject to EU and British but not American sanctions have continued to ship Russian oil unimpeded. As of today, the shadow fleet constitutes around two-thirds of the tanker traffic out of Russia’s Baltic ports, which makes up about half the country’s seaborne oil exports.
The Trump administration did sanction Russia’s two largest oil producers, Lukoil and Rosneft, in October 2025, which drove down the price of Russian oil. But it undid that progress a few months later by granting multiple waivers to buyers of Russian oil as global prices were rising amid the war with Iran. With these waivers in place and much of the shadow fleet operational, Russia was soon able to export oil on its own terms and profit from the price spikes. By April, the discount on Russian oil relative to global prices had all but vanished. Moscow’s oil tax revenues from April through July were $14 billion higher than they were a year earlier.
To put real pressure on Russia’s oil revenues, Western countries must defang the shadow fleet. Washington has been dragging its heels on sanctioning additional vessels in the fleet, however, and a new piece of legislation, the so-called Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act—approved by a wide margin by the Senate in August and currently under consideration in the House of Representatives—will probably not make a significant difference. The bill would give the executive branch new authority to impose tariffs on importers of Russian oil, but there is little reason to think this would have much effect; the Trump administration’s 25 percent tariff on India has not stopped the country from importing Russian oil. Although the bill would pave the way for the United States to sanction shadow fleet vessels directly, the Trump administration has so far refused to enact such measures and may continue to do so.
That leaves the task of taking on the shadow fleet to Europe. Earlier EU and British sanctions on their own have not meaningfully restricted Russian exports, but that is only because Europe has left critical gaps in its enforcement regime.
It is now time to close those gaps, starting with the continued supply of Greek and other oil tankers to Russia. The ships in the shadow fleet are around five years older than the average operational oil tanker because their owners want to minimize their losses in the event the ships are sanctioned. As these vessels approach the end of their service lives, keeping the fleet’s numbers steady requires frequent replacements. Until now, the single largest source of those replacements has been Greek ship owners. The EU forbade sales of such tankers to Russian nationals and entities in a sanctions package introduced in December 2023, but European vessels are still making their way to Russian buyers. Brussels now needs to extend the prohibition to any transaction conducted through holding companies that ends in the transfer of a vessel to the shadow fleet. New regulations should oblige European vessel owners to sell only to reputable buyers approved jointly by the EU and the United Kingdom and to provide tracking information for vessels after they are sold. Of course, there are many other sellers from whom Russia can buy tankers, but finding alternatives for such a large number of its purchases would be more costly and take more time.
Europe has substantial economic power and a strong legal system, and it can use both to impose consequences on third countries that enable the shadow fleet’s operations. To hide their connection to Russia, ships in the shadow fleet are usually flagged in other countries—ones that do not require tankers to hold insurance. International maritime treaties, however, allow states to demand that vessels navigating their territorial waters adhere to certain requirements, including coverage by a reputable insurer. The EU and the United Kingdom should pressure flag states to enforce those rules. They could threaten to cut aid to countries that fail to verify the insurance coverage of the ships they register, for instance, or make clear that these countries could face legal action in the event of an oil spill or other accident. If flag states start enforcing insurance requirements, many of Russia’s aging tankers would be rendered obsolete because they are insufficiently seaworthy to be covered by reputable insurers. And because Western companies dominate the shipping insurance market, most of the ships that qualify for insurance plans would purchase them from Western firms, making it easier to enforce the G-7 oil price cap.
European countries would also have legal grounds to interdict old, poorly maintained ships that pose immediate environmental dangers. Such action is not as escalatory as it may sound. Countries including Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, and the United Kingdom have all stopped, inspected, and occasionally seized shadow fleet vessels over the past two years, but these interdictions have yet to invite any overt retaliation by Russia.
Cutting off Russia’s supply of ships and forcing vessels to meet the regulatory requirements of Western insurers would go a long way toward reducing the shadow fleet’s evasion of price caps. Once those means of enforcement are in place, Europe can then go further in restricting Russia’s oil profits by lowering the price caps on refined products. Right now, the caps on high- and low-value refined products are set at fixed dollar amounts that are well below market prices, but the EU and the United Kingdom should have a plan in place for adjusting the caps after the Strait of Hormuz reopens and oil prices normalize. The preferred model should be the cap on crude prices established in 2025, set at 15 percent below the market prices over the previous six months. An automatic adjustment of this kind would allow Europe to offer consistent guidance to well-intentioned companies engaged in the oil trade and to accommodate frequent swings in energy prices without needing every EU member state to approve every change to fixed-rate price caps.
EU policymakers have little to lose from implementing these measures. They are designed not to confront Russia directly, but instead to focus Europe’s coercive power on flag states and on ship owners inside the EU. If applied correctly, they should not result in increased global energy prices, either, because they would preserve Russia’s volume of exports. But Moscow’s revenues from those exports would be limited, because more of the Russian oil trade would be pushed from the shadow fleet to legitimate tankers that are subject to European price caps. Until now, Europe has been reluctant to expand its sanctions on Russia, for fear that such steps could be escalatory. But policymakers’ appetite for bolder measures is growing amid the United States’ inaction, Russia’s increasingly effective evasion of sanctions, and rising concern that the war could spread beyond Ukraine.
The absence of action, meanwhile, hands Moscow an easy win. Russia will continue to replace aging tankers with newer ones and collect enormous oil profits from maritime trade that will feed directly into its war machine in Ukraine. Europe has policy levers it can pull to stop the shadow fleet, and that is an opportunity it cannot afford to pass up.
articles.summary: How Europe can disrupt Moscow’s oil windfall.

articles.title: How al-Qaeda Ended
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
AUDREY KURTH CRONIN is Director of the Carnegie Mellon Institute for Strategy and Technology. She is the author of How Terrorism Ends: Understanding the Decline and Demise of Terrorist Campaigns.
Al-Qaeda has ended. The organization that Osama bin Laden founded and led, that attacked the United States 25 years ago and killed 2,977 innocent Americans in the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and rural Pennsylvania, no longer survives—and U.S. officials should say so, instead of burnishing the group’s legacy by acting and speaking as if it still exists. Terrorism has not ceased, jihadism has not gone away, and the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran may ignite more anti-American sentiment and violence. But the group that attacked the United States on 9/11 is finished.
In the years following that assault, thousands of Americans dedicated their lives to avenging the victims. The nationwide horror of watching planes go into towers—innocent people crushed, burned, or jumping to their deaths—catalyzed a passionate response. And the cost to those who responded was high: in the post-9/11 wars, more than 15,000 U.S. military members and contractors died in combat, and some 1.8 million became disabled. And from 2012 to 2021, four times as many active-duty or veteran military members died by suicide as died in combat. Service members from loyal U.S. allies, especially Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, and the United Kingdom, joined the United States in combat; hundreds of them died fighting alongside Americans. They and their families deserve to know their efforts were not in vain. Washington and its allies lost the war in Afghanistan but succeeded against al-Qaeda.
Jihadist terrorism persists as a threat, and not every group using the name “al-Qaeda” has been neutralized. Dangerous organizations operate in the Arabian Peninsula, the Horn of Africa, North Africa, the Sahel, and South Asia. They carry out attacks and hold territory, and some have come close to taking down governments, especially in Mali, Somalia, and Yemen. Jihadists of various stripes train in Taliban-governed Afghanistan—a development that must be closely monitored. But none of what are sometimes called “al-Qaeda affiliates” is centrally directed or led by bin Laden’s organization, and officials should cease suggesting they are, since doing so inflates the threat they pose without making it any easier to combat them. Indeed, it would be best to cease using the term “al-Qaeda affiliate” altogether.
Studying the pattern of attacks tied directly to al-Qaeda shows how the central organization ran out of steam. Before 9/11, the core al-Qaeda organization kept up a steady pace of global operations against U.S. targets, with a track record that included the 1993 bombing of the World Trade Center (six dead, more than 1,000 injured), the 1996 bombing of Khobar Towers (19 killed, hundreds injured), the 1998 bombing of the U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania (224 killed, thousands injured), and the 2000 attack on the USS Cole (17 killed). After 2001, core al-Qaeda’s efforts against the U.S. homeland included a fumbled 2001 attempt to ignite a bomb placed in a shoe on an airliner bound for Miami and a failed 2009 suicide bombing plot targeting the New York City subway. The group caused more pain for U.S. friends and allies than for the United States itself, with deadly attacks in Bali in 2002, Riyadh in 2003, and London in 2005. But following that spike in the first decade of the twenty-first century, the momentum shifted to other jihadist groups, and after 2009, core al-Qaeda’s global operations essentially ceased.
For decades, I have studied how terrorist groups end, based on a dataset of 457 terrorist campaigns and organizations going back a century. By analyzing their makeup, targets, and intended audiences, one can identify common trajectories. Although not mutually exclusive, there are six major pathways such groups ultimately take: decapitation, negotiation, success, failure, repression, and reorientation to another mode of operation (such as ordinary criminality or insurgency). In the case of core al-Qaeda, although decapitation and military repression played important roles, the group ended primarily through strategic failure—just as bin Laden feared it would.
In the aftermath of the 9/11 attacks, the U.S. campaign should have been focused on destroying the perpetrators. But the United States failed to clearly define the threat. The Authorization for the Use of Military Force that Congress passed on September 14, 2001, did not mention al-Qaeda at all, instead vaguely identifying Washington’s enemies as “those nations, organizations or persons [the president] determines planned, authorized, committed or aided the terrorist attacks that occurred on September 11, 2001.” A few days later, President George W. Bush echoed that framing. “Our war on al-Qaeda begins with al-Qaeda but it does not end there,” he declared. “It will not end until every terrorist group of global reach has been found, stopped, and defeated.”
With that, the United States declared war on a tactic, one that had shaped political violence in the modern world since anarchist terrorism swept through Europe before World War I. Washington had set itself a task it could never accomplish. Making the enemy “terrorism” meant its efforts would lack clarity and drag on endlessly. What followed was an ill-focused campaign in Afghanistan (which removed the Taliban from power in Kabul but allowed bin Laden and his cronies to escape) and then the war in Iraq, where al-Qaeda had not even operated until an affiliate emerged after the U.S. military occupation had been in place for a year. The invasion of Iraq did more to prolong the life of al-Qaeda than any other single event, drawing fresh recruits from Sunni populations all over the world, and eventually creating the conditions for the emergence of the Islamic State organization.
Still, in the 25 years that followed, sometimes almost despite itself, the United States along with its allies did defeat bin Laden’s al-Qaeda—often with inadvertent help from the group itself. An important factor was the May 2011 killing of Osama bin Laden in Abbottabad, Pakistan, an event that undermined al-Qaeda’s coherence. U.S. forces stormed bin Laden’s compound, killed him, and then helicoptered his body to an aircraft carrier and buried it at sea, leaving no possibility for a memorial or focal point for his followers. The documents recovered in that raid were just as valuable to U.S. counterterrorism as bin Laden’s death, offering compelling evidence that he had not been centrally directing the group’s operations for some time. His death did not end al-Qaeda, but it was justice served, and it undercut the ability of his fans to rally around him.
By September 2011, U.S. officials were claiming that the number of surviving people directly connected to carrying out the 9/11 attacks was no more than a couple of dozen. But instead of declaring victory over the group at that point and moving on, the U.S. drone campaign, which had begun in 2002 under Bush and accelerated in the early Obama administration, expanded its scope and target set. Instead of so-called personality attacks (which target known leaders), the campaign shifted to “signature strikes,” targeting unidentified individuals or groups who fit a particular profile, not just in Afghanistan and Pakistan but also in Somalia and Yemen. The drone campaign degraded al-Qaeda’s ranks and avenged attempted attacks—for example, by eliminating members of al-Qaeda’s Yemen affiliate who trained and equipped Umar Farouk Abdulmutallab, the would-be “underwear bomber” who tried to bring down a civilian airliner in 2009. But drone attacks also catalyzed terrorism: according to declassified FBI interviews, the 2013 Boston Marathon bomber, Tamerlan Tsarnaev (likewise inspired by al-Qaeda’s Yemen affiliate), told a friend that his killing of an eight-year-old in that attack was justified because children in Afghanistan and Pakistan had been killed by U.S. drones. The drone campaign had a strategic impact on U.S. allies: public attitudes in France, Germany, Spain, Turkey, and the United Kingdom hardened against Washington’s “global war on terrorism.” Drones were tactically important and probably saved lives, but they did not end al-Qaeda.
More critical to that success was intelligence and law-enforcement collaboration among U.S. allies, which remains the bedrock of American counterterrorism. New measures to curb terrorist financing, biometric screening and databases, and new ways of sharing intelligence among allies helped Washington monitor threats beyond American shores. In 2006, for example, close cooperation between U.S. and British intelligence services thwarted an al-Qaeda-linked plot to smuggle the explosive TATP in beverage containers and take down U.S.-bound civilian aircraft over the Atlantic.
But much of the damage al-Qaeda suffered was self-inflicted. A key driver was a backlash against terrorist attacks that hurt Muslim civilians and a resulting loss of support among communities al-Qaeda supposedly represented. Bin Laden knew this was a weakness, and his frustration shows in the communications discovered in the Abbottabad compound. A May 2010 letter he wrote to one of his deputies warns, “This is when we lose the perception of the Muslims towards us, which is that we are the ones defending the Muslims and fighting their biggest enemy, the Crusader Zionist alliance…[and instead] killing those that the general public consider Muslims.” Al-Qaeda started building global franchises in 2004, but they typically emerged out of existing organizations, and their operational ties to core al-Qaeda could be hazy. According to bin Laden’s own assessment, rogue affiliates hurt al-Qaeda’s cause more than they helped it, since most victims of their violence were Muslim civilians, whose families and communities then blamed al-Qaeda. According to the Pew Global Attitudes project, between 2003 and 2011, support for bin Laden personally had dropped in Indonesia from 59 percent to 26 percent, in Jordan from 56 percent to 13 percent, and in the Palestinian territories from 72 percent to 34 percent. In Pakistan, where bin Laden was hiding, support for him plunged from 46 percent in 2003 to 18 percent in 2010. A decade after 9/11, bin Laden’s dream of a vanguard uniting Muslims had evaporated.
Internal divisions also played a role in al-Qaeda’s demise. The most dramatic split was with the Islamic State, or ISIS, which had started out as an al-Qaeda affiliate before rebranding. In 2014, ISIS conquered major parts of Iraq and Syria, drawing some 15,000 foreign fighters from 80 countries to join its self-declared caliphate. This was a huge challenge to the original group: al-Qaeda had ideas, but ISIS had territory.
ISIS’s trajectory reflected the core problem of dealing with affiliates who did not share (or necessarily even grasp) bin Laden’s strategy. In 2005, bin Laden’s chief deputy, Ayman al-Zawahiri, wrote to Abu Musab al-Zarqawi—the leader of what was then known as al-Qaeda in Iraq and would eventually become ISIS—advising him to stop killing Shiite civilians and beheading hostages in grotesque videos. “Among the things which the feelings of the Muslim populace who love and support you will never find palatable … are the scenes of slaughtering the hostages,” Zawahiri wrote. “We don’t need this.” Zarqawi ignored him. In 2006, a U.S. airstrike killed Zarqawi. But for the next decade, global jihadism shifted firmly in his direction, and against the comparatively more cautious approach of al-Qaeda.
Even as ISIS swamped al-Qaeda, however, the limits of its approach became clear, vindicating Zawahiri’s warning. The first mistake ISIS made was to gather forces and materiel in a concentrated space, becoming a perfect target for conventional military force. Its second error was to enthusiastically embrace gruesome forms of brutality and sadism, antagonizing virtually everyone who did not belong to the group; by 2016, almost the entire world had united against it. Working with Iraqi, Kurdish, and Syrian forces, a global coalition to defeat ISIS had by 2019 recaptured the territory the group had seized and destroyed the caliphate. But for al-Qaeda, the damage had been done: it had lost its foothold in Iraq and split its recruitment base with a younger, flashier brand. Zawahiri’s response was to decentralize and focus on groups in South Asia and North Africa, such as al-Qaeda in the Indian Subcontinent and al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb, which primarily sought to overthrow local governments.
In July 2022, nearly a year after the American withdrawal from Afghanistan, a U.S. drone strike in Kabul killed Zawahiri. The muted response to his death confirmed the weakness of core al-Qaeda. Today, the apparent head of al-Qaeda is Said al-Adel, who lives in Iran, a Shiite-majority country where, for a decade after 9/11, he and other al-Qaeda leaders and their families spent years living under a form of house arrest, and where his room to maneuver remains strictly limited. He has not even declared himself the group’s leader, perhaps because he fears assassination—but perhaps because there is, in reality, nothing for him to lead.
Although the group could one day reinvent itself or carry out attacks sponsored or abetted by Iran, the al-Qaeda that attacked the United States 25 years ago has ended. The United States sometimes accelerated and sometimes slowed the group’s demise. But ultimately, al-Qaeda failed.
articles.summary: Terrorists sometimes defeat themselves.

articles.title: The Rise and Fall of Global Jihadism
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
DANIEL BYMAN is a Professor in the School of Foreign Service at Georgetown University and Director of the Warfare, Irregular Threats, and Terrorism Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Twenty-five years ago, members of the jihadi group al-Qaeda hijacked four American airplanes, flying two of them into the World Trade Center towers in New York City and one into the Pentagon, in Washington, D.C. Passengers attempted to seize control of the fourth plane, and it crashed in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, killing everyone aboard. The hijackers killed 2,977 people in total—by far the deadliest single terrorist attack in history. To many Americans, the events of September 11, 2001, seemed to come out of nowhere. Few had even heard of al-Qaeda before the attacks. Yet by September 12, the United States had plunged into what President George W. Bush called “a war against terrorism,” a fight that would persist for decades, ensnare multiple jihadi groups, and extend to all corners of the earth.
The United States had many setbacks in this war. The ways in which it attempted to prevent another 9/11, or an even larger-scale attack, entailed massive, often inefficient investments as well as troop losses. Some of its efforts, such as the full-scale wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, were brutally destructive. The 2003 invasion of Iraq, in particular, drove a surge in jihadi recruitment. In the years since 2001, various new jihadi groups—some of them connected to al-Qaeda, some opposed to it—have set up shop in the Middle East and across East and West Africa, where they have fueled bloody civil wars, shattered local communities, and launched terrorist attacks both in the region and outside it.
But the war on terrorism has not been a complete failure, either. Al-Qaeda itself is devastated. There have been few jihadi attacks on U.S. territory—perhaps the most important measure of success for most American leaders—in the past two and a half decades. According to New America Foundation data, jihadi terrorists have killed 122 people in the United States since 2001, a fraction of what U.S. officials feared in the aftermath of 9/11. And although jihadi groups survive, jihadism has lost much of its ideological salience.
Consider what has happened since 2023. On October 7, Hamas, a group that al-Qaeda regularly criticized for compromising on theological principles in the pursuit of its political agenda, launched a bloody terrorist attack on Israel, killing more than 1,100 people. Israel went on to kill tens of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza, many of them civilians, and conduct other attacks in Iraq, Lebanon, Syria, and the West Bank. In 2025, the United States joined Israel in bombing Iran, and in 2026 the United States and Israel launched a full-scale war with the initial objective of regime change in Tehran. The Israeli war in Gaza led to mass protests around the world, and all of these events offered fodder for conspiracy theories about the enemies of Islam plotting against Muslims. Yet in contrast to the 2003 U.S. invasion of Iraq or the onset of the Syrian civil war in 2011, they have triggered no jihadi surge. Indeed, the former jihadis who overthrew the Syrian dictator Bashar al-Assad, in 2024, quickly sought to make nice with states that have long fought terror organizations, including the United States and Saudi Arabia, upon taking power.
A quarter century after Osama bin Laden gave the order for the 9/11 attacks, his successors have not built a durable transnational movement capable of repeatedly attacking the United States and forcing governments to bend to their demands. The sense of historic possibility that once made the jihadi movement so threatening to Western countries has faded. The United States may not have won the war on terrorism, but the jihadis clearly lost.
In late 2001, al-Qaeda appeared ascendant. The movement grew out of the armed struggle against the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan in the 1980s, and it attracted Muslim fighters from around the world. Under bin Laden’s leadership, al-Qaeda had many goals, including helping the Taliban secure power in Afghanistan and training its members for terrorist and insurgent campaigns throughout the Muslim world, but ousting the United States from the Middle East was at the top of the list. Other jihadis prioritized fighting governments that they saw as foreign invaders in Chechnya and Kashmir, toppling supposedly apostate Arab regimes, battling Shiite Muslims, or creating a caliphate.
The scale of its attack on the United States gave al-Qaeda an aura of momentum and outsize influence within the jihadi movement and beyond. After 9/11, the movement grew in stature, and fighting the United States and its Western allies, which most jihadis had previously considered a relatively low priority, became a more mainstream objective. The fact that the U.S. government would make few distinctions between al-Qaeda-linked groups and jihadis with a more local focus in its subsequent counterterrorism campaign only reinforced that trend.
Several factors had made the 2001 attacks possible. Among them were the many shortcomings in Washington’s approach to counterterrorism, including the mistakes identified by the 9/11 Commission, an independent body set up by the U.S. government in 2002, on which I served as a staff member. Those included poor information sharing among U.S. government agencies, a failure to place on watchlists future hijackers who were suspected of links to al-Qaeda and were believed to be traveling to the United States, a lackadaisical effort to find suspected terrorists believed to be in the United States already, and no response to alarming field officer reports that jihadis appeared to be interested in learning how to fly planes.
Just as important was al-Qaeda’s own organizing. Most of its leaders were creative, dedicated, and willing to work with other groups, giving the movement a large network from which to recruit the best operatives. Critically, al-Qaeda also had a safe haven in Taliban-ruled Afghanistan, from which it could strategize, plot attacks, and coordinate with its international partners without interference. The CIA estimated that 10,000 to 20,000 volunteers attended training camps in Afghanistan in the late 1990s, enabling al-Qaeda to build a small army. Recruits from all over the world, but especially the Middle East, learned the basics of insurgent war. The more promising candidates learned advanced counterintelligence and bomb-making techniques. Some of those who received training went to fight alongside the Taliban against the group’s remaining enemies inside Afghanistan, and the Taliban permitted others to leave the country and rejoin local insurgent groups or terrorist cells around the world.
Standout recruits among the mass of volunteers were selected for additional training and assigned to high-priority operations. Many of the 9/11 hijackers, for instance, initially went to Afghanistan with the intention to acquire skills and connections before traveling onward to Chechnya to fight alongside Chechen insurgents against Russian security forces. After they were indoctrinated in the camps, al-Qaeda sent them to attack the United States instead.
Most governments around the world paid limited attention to this growing danger and did little to prevent members of terrorist organizations from recruiting, generating propaganda, fundraising, and networking on their soil as long as they did not carry out attacks there. Various jihadi leaders and operatives planned operations in Algeria, Bosnia, and elsewhere from London in the 1990s, for example. Even the United States was relatively lax; Ayman al-Zawahiri, who took over al-Qaeda after U.S. forces killed bin Laden in 2011, had come to the country in the 1990s to fundraise.
After 9/11, the United States’ counterterrorism efforts quickly succeeded in dismantling al-Qaeda’s base of operations. As the wreckage of the World Trade Center’s Twin Towers smoldered, the United States commenced military operations in Afghanistan. CIA officers and special operations forces, working with anti-Taliban groups and bolstered by U.S. airpower, quickly overthrew the Taliban. Many al-Qaeda members died in the fight. Those who survived lost their safe haven and, critically, their training camps, and were forced to flee. Most went to Pakistan and Iran and carried on the group’s operations from there; most of al-Qaeda’s most successful post–9/11 attacks, such as the 2005 bombings of London’s transportation system, were orchestrated from Pakistan. But both Islamabad and Tehran were less accommodating hosts than the Taliban were. Neither allowed al-Qaeda to establish new training camps, and Pakistani authorities, in particular, regularly helped the United States arrest and kill the group’s operatives.
Without the large-scale training infrastructure that al-Qaeda had set up in Afghanistan, jihadi groups lost much of their ability to mount as sophisticated or distant an attack as 9/11, but they continued to terrorize local populations across the broader Middle East. The United States gave the jihadi cause new energy with its 2003 invasion of Iraq, a war justified in part by the need to confront terrorism. The subsequent U.S. occupation incited anger across the region and fueled the growth of anti-U.S. militant groups in Iraq.
The chaos unleashed by the 2011 Arab uprisings gave these and other groups even more room to grow. The eventual outcome was the rise of the so-called Islamic State (or ISIS), which at its height in 2014–15 controlled territory in Iraq and Syria roughly the size of Virginia and home to millions of people. It attracted tens of thousands more recruits from countries in the Middle East, Europe, and Central Asia. Other groups, such as al-Shabab, in Somalia, also came to hold territory where they taxed and menaced the population and planned their operations.
Yet persistent American pressure on the remaining jihadi havens bore fruit over time. In Iraq and Syria, the United States steadily eroded the Islamic State’s control until the group lost the last of its territory. Unlike in the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, which involved tens of thousands of U.S. forces, Washington deployed small special operations teams while local partners, trained by U.S. forces and backed by U.S. airpower and intelligence, did most of the fighting (and the dying). In other places such as Libya and Somalia, Washington supported the national armies and local militias battling jihadi forces and engaged in whack-a-mole with jihadi leaders. The advent of the armed drone aided this effort, enabling the U.S. military to gather more intelligence and strike more quickly, and with less collateral damage, compared with traditional airpower. Increased cooperation with allied intelligence services helped, as well. Much of this work was mechanical and humdrum—for instance, linking a phone number here to a financial transaction there—but it allowed Washington and its partners to uncover and unravel much of the global jihadi web, arresting members of al-Qaeda and other groups and disrupting their operations around the world.
No less consequential were massive U.S. investments in homeland security. The Department of Homeland Security, created in 2002, was meant to bring together airport security, border protection, and other parts of the national security apparatus that would be involved in preventing terrorist attacks on U.S. territory. Increased spending at airports, on disaster response, and on improved communication between federal, state, and local officials was meant to ensure that information about new threats would be shared quickly, that terrorists would be prevented from entering the country, and that the response to any future attack would be better coordinated. The FBI made counterterrorism a top priority, and it aggressively investigated individuals suspected of terrorist activity. At times it was too aggressive; civil liberties organizations contend that the bureau detained and questioned large numbers of Muslim men and monitored mosques without evidence of wrongdoing. But overall, the effort was effective at preventing attacks.
Each measure bolstered the others. Without training camps, would-be terrorists had no place to gain skills and network. Insufficient training could make them more prone to small mistakes that made their fundraising and recruiting efforts more easily detected. More active U.S. and allied security services would be ready to catch them, and then make the intelligence they gathered from those they arrested available to help target overseas networks and havens.
The erosion of jihadis’ havens in Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria, and elsewhere steadily damaged the groups’ credibility and appeal. At the height of the Islamic State’s power, holding territory demonstrated its prowess and attracted followers who wanted to live in a place governed by the group’s version of Islamic law. But when the Islamic State lost territory, its calls for new fighters to come to defend its self-declared caliphate began to ring hollow. Recruitment became much harder. Fewer and fewer would-be jihadis wanted to join a group that increasingly looked like it was losing.
It was not only U.S. pressure that brought about the decline of jihadism. The jihadis themselves repeatedly made choices that reduced their appeal. For one, they made too many enemies. Al-Qaeda’s foes included not just the United States but also other supposed foreign occupiers, such as India, Israel, and Russia. Some strands within the broader movement also opposed regimes in Muslim countries that they considered impious, including the governments of Egypt, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, and Yemen. The Islamic State’s list of foes was even longer; it fought most fiercely against Shiites and other non-Sunni Muslims.
Declaring so many enemies enabled these groups to attract a wide variety of followers, but it also meant that they diffused their energy. Attacking everyone everywhere all at once made it difficult to put sustained effort into achieving any single goal. Even more damning, it ensured that everyone would attack them. Fighting jihadi terrorism was one of the few causes that united countries around the world, and the United States was able to solicit support for its intelligence and military campaigns from foreign governments that disagreed with Washington on many issues but shared an interest in quashing these groups.
Even more consequentially, some jihadi groups turned Muslim publics against them by mistreating Muslim civilians. People who might have been sympathetic to their fights against the United States and other foreign powers did not approve of jihadis’ killing of Saudi police and security officials in 2003 and 2004, for instance, or of an al-Qaeda affiliate’s slaughter of both Sunni and Shiite civilians in Iraq in 2006 and 2007. Such killings diminished the jihadis’ influence. In Saudi Arabia, the government, with the broad support of the public, killed or arrested al-Qaeda members, devastating the group’s operations in the country. In Iraq, the faction earned rebukes from clerics who had previously supported global jihad as well as from more mainstream religious leaders.
The Islamic State’s overreach in Iraq and Syria was ultimately its undoing. Its declaration of a caliphate in 2014 was electrifying to many Muslims, coming at a time when the group seemed to be successfully expanding its borders and fighting off enemies. Yet the project created the conditions for the group’s eventual defeat. As bin Laden himself had privately warned another jihadi leader in Yemen years earlier, building a state would give the United States and other countries a place to concentrate their firepower. When the Islamic State declared its caliphate, not only did its territorial control make the group easier to target but its governing also exposed the group’s brutality. Its maximalist claims also made it impossible to work with other jihadis, let alone other countries.
By the mid-2020s, the jihadi movement was in no position to capitalize on upheaval in the Middle East. The war in Gaza, the fall of Assad to former jihadis, and the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran all supplied the kinds of grievances, images, and narratives that once fueled the movement’s global spread. But with the important exception of Somalia and large parts of West Africa, jihadi groups have not managed a mobilization comparable with the ones after the 2003 Iraq War or during the rise of the Islamic State. At those times, their ideology still had international momentum. Yet after the definitive collapse of the Islamic State’s territorial project, in most places the idea of global jihad lost its former appeal. The past few years might have provided an ideal opportunity to recruit disaffected Muslim youth in Europe and the Middle East, but the jihadis could not seize the moment.
Despite the decline of jihadism and the relative safety of U.S. territory from attack after 9/11, it is difficult to claim that the United States won its war on terrorism. Neither major war fought under that banner, those in Afghanistan and Iraq, ended well. U.S. forces swiftly removed the Taliban from power in Afghanistan, eliminating the safe haven jihadis had enjoyed, but the campaign turned into a grinding stalemate and then, in 2021, a humiliating defeat when a reconstituted Taliban retook control of the country. The war in Iraq eventually allowed a better government than Saddam Hussein’s dictatorship to emerge, but it also set the groundwork for the rise of the Islamic State. These and other wars in the region came at a huge human cost, too. The Brown University Costs of War project has estimated that almost a million people, nearly half of them civilians, died in Afghanistan, Iraq, Pakistan, Syria, and Yemen between 2001 and 2023. The United States lost more than 2,000 soldiers in Afghanistan and more than 4,000 in Iraq, and more than 50,000 were wounded between the two conflicts. Washington spent $8 trillion on its post-9/11 wars through 2021.
Counterterrorism efforts did not stop jihadism entirely, either. For years, U.S. military campaigns and effective al-Qaeda and Islamic State propaganda amplifying American and allied abuses kept alive the political conditions that enabled the ideology’s spread. And although no jihadi group was able to carry out another operation on the scale of 9/11, the United States and its allies were the target of numerous plots and attacks by individuals who were inspired by jihadi ideology even if they had never met an al-Qaeda or Islamic State member. Many attempted attacks have been foiled thanks to better countermeasures, but the desire to kill Americans and citizens of other countries on jihadi groups’ lists of enemies has not gone away. Efforts by successive U.S. administrations to take on jihadi propaganda directly—including numerous programs aimed at “countering violent extremism”—were not particularly effective at winning the hearts and minds of people who opposed U.S. policy and were disinclined to trust the United States while Muslim civilians were dying in its wars.
The persistence of an ideology is not the same as salience, however. At their height, jihadi groups proved capable of spectacular violence, forming alliances amid civil wars and even seizing territory. But they failed to translate those achievements into a durable political project or sustained global appeal. Outside sub-Saharan Africa, jihadism no longer offers anything like the same persuasive answer to Muslim grievances or plausible path to political transformation that it did in the first two decades of this century. Jihadis are not flocking to battle Israel or the United States, and the former Syrian jihadis sitting in Damascus seem to prefer attracting foreign investment to fighting infidel powers.
This leaves Washington with tough decisions about how far it should go to fight the jihadi groups that remain active today. Most of them have survived by getting involved in civil wars that have been highly destructive but have erupted in places that are peripheral to U.S. interests, such as Mali, Somalia, and Yemen. There is a risk that jihadi groups could turn their involvement in these wars into opportunities to create new safe havens from which to organize international attacks. But if the United States attacks them directly, it also risks inviting retaliation and getting bogged down in new conflicts. In places such as Somalia and Yemen, Washington’s solution has been to launch drone attacks on jihadi leaders and operatives and provide limited support to regional governments, warlords, and tribal leaders to keep jihadi groups off balance.
